question: Give me a list of AIGA Medal awardees awarded from 2022 to 2014 who were awarded posthumously 20 years or more after their death. In the case of someone dying in the same year that the award is given, treat this as not posthumous. If two people were given a joint medal, if either one of them died prior then you should treat this as posthumous, and you should list the entry as a single entry for any joint awardees. Present the list in alphabetical order by first name.

Give me a list of AIGA Medal awardees awarded from 2022 to 2014 who were awarded posthumously 20 years or more after their death. If two people were given a joint medal, if either one of them died prior then you should treat this as posthumous, and you should list the entry as a single entry for any joint awardees. Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-2) the [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication")."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.

Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

Award

| American Institute of Graphic Arts medal |
| --- |
| [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a7/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts_medal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts_medal.jpg) The physical medal was designed by sculptor [James Earle Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Earle_Fraser_(sculptor) "James Earle Fraser (sculptor)") in 1920.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-1) |
| Awarded for | Exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication") |
| Presented by | [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) |
| First award | 1920;106 years ago(1920) |
| Website | [www.aiga.org](http://www.aiga.org/) |

Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-2) the [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication")."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.

Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

**Michael Patrick Cronan** (June 9, 1951 – January 1, 2013)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:6-1) was an American graphic designer, brand strategist, adjunct professor, and fine art painter. He was one of the founders of the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area")[postmodern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodern "Postmodern") movement in [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design"), that later became known as the "Pacific Wave".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)

He was a 2014 [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) Medalist and received the AIGA lifetime achievement award in 2009.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Cronan was born in San Francisco, California on June 9, 1951 and grew up near [Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento "Sacramento").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2) As a teenager, he learned [letterpress printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letterpress_printing "Letterpress printing") and had become an artist in a local print shop, creating posters.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)

He studied fine art at [California College of Arts and Crafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_College_of_Arts_and_Crafts "California College of Arts and Crafts") (now known as California College of the Arts) and later graduated from [California State University, Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Sacramento "California State University, Sacramento") (BA degree 1974).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-4) He met his future wife and business partner, Karin Hibma at California State University, Sacramento.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3) Together they had two sons, sculptor and artist, Shawn HibmaCronan; and industrial designer, Nick Cronan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-5)

In 1971, he went abroad to study archeology, and work as an archaeological dig manager for [Hebrew University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_University "Hebrew University") in the [Negev Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negev_Desert "Negev Desert") and then at the [Dead Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea "Dead Sea").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Pacific Wave movement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pacific Wave movement")]

In the early 1980s a few San Francisco–based designers were nicknamed “The Michaels” because they all had the same name (Cronan, alongside [Mabry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Mabry "Michael Mabry"), [Manwaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Manwaring "Michael Manwaring"), [Vanderbyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Vanderbyl "Michael Vanderbyl"), [Schwab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schwab_(designer) "Michael Schwab (designer)")), and later they were known as the "Pacific Wave" according to historian [Steven Heller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Heller_(design_writer) "Steven Heller (design writer)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:3-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-8)

### Cronan Design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cronan Design")]

Cronan and Karin Hibma established Michael Patrick Cronan Design (also known as Cronan Design, but later known simply as Cronan) in 1980.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:2-9) Cronan Design clients including [TiVo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TiVo "TiVo"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)[Kindle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindle_Store "Kindle Store"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10) Good Belly,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)[Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:5-11)[Levi Strauss & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi_Strauss_&_Co. "Levi Strauss & Co."),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:5-11)[Estee Lauder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A9e_Lauder_Companies "Estée Lauder Companies"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:5-11) among others. Cronan Design often worked on [brand-strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_management "Brand management") consulting, they would extensively interview clients and Cronan found naming inspiration by playing with _[Scrabble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrabble "Scrabble")_ tiles for unique letter combinations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:6-1)

In June 2009, he and Karin Hibma were named as two of [Fast Company's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Company_(magazine) "Fast Company (magazine)") list of 100 Most Creative People in Business.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-12)

### Walking Man

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Walking Man")]

Together Cronan and Hibma formed a sub-brand of clothing design, Walking Man, in 1989.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:2-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-13) In 1992 and 1993, Walking Man clothing won the [I.D. Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.D._(magazine) "I.D. (magazine)") Consumer Product of the Year/Gold Award presented at the [Cooper Hewitt National Design Museum, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper-Hewitt,_National_Design_Museum "Cooper-Hewitt, National Design Museum").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Other design experiences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Other design experiences")]

He was an [adjunct professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjunct_professor "Adjunct professor") of graphic design at California College of the Arts from 1981–2001.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Cronan designed the stamp commemorating the fiftieth anniversary of NATO and later the Prostate Awareness stamp for the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service").[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_][[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)

In 1998, SFMOMA commissioned Cronan to create the SFMOMA symbol which graphically captures the distinctive oculus at the center of the museum building designed by [Mario Botta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Botta "Mario Botta").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Alongside his design work, Cronan had worked as a fine art painter for most of his life.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-14)

His graphic design work is included in many public museum collections including at the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Art "Los Angeles County Museum of Art") (LACMA),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-15) San Francisco Museum of Modern Art,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-16) the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-17) among others.

## Membership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Membership")]

Cronan was a founding member of the [American Institute of Graphic Art (AIGA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA "AIGA") chapter in San Francisco[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3) and the AIGASF chapter president after serving on the AIGA national board for three years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Cronan was Chairman of the Board of the [Pickle Family Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickle_Family_Circus "Pickle Family Circus"), attended the Aspen Leadership Summit in 2005 and served on the Board of the Aspen Design Summit from 2005 – 2006.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

*   1985 – _[Pacific Wave](http://designarchives.aiga.org/#/entries/Pacific%20Wave%20Museo%3A%20Fortuny/\_/detail/relevance/asc/0/7/5029/pacific-wave-museo-fortuny/1)_, curated by Giorgio Camuffo, at [Museo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortuny_Museum "Fortuny Museum"), [Venice, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice,_Italy "Venice, Italy")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:3-6)
*   1993 – _In the Public Eye: The Work of Four Graphic Designers_, [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art") (SFMOMA), San Francisco, California. This exhibition was including Michael Manwaring, [Gerald Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Reis?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gerald Reis (page does not exist)"), and [Michael Vanderbyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Vanderbyl "Michael Vanderbyl"). It was the first graphic design exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and its popularity ushered in an expanded presence of graphics in the museum's floor space and permanent collection.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   2002 – _US Design: 1975-2000_, curated by R. Craig Miller, [Denver Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Art_Museum "Denver Art Museum"), Denver, Colorado[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-18)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Death")]

On January 1, 2013, Cronan died at his [Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley,_California "Berkeley, California") home after a long time with colon cancer.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-19) He had been diagnosed for the same for five years previously.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3)

**Michael Patrick Cronan** (June 9, 1951 – January 1, 2013)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:6-1) was an American graphic designer, brand strategist, adjunct professor, and fine art painter. He was one of the founders of the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area")[postmodern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodern "Postmodern") movement in [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design"), that later became known as the "Pacific Wave".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)

He was a 2014 [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) Medalist and received the AIGA lifetime achievement award in 2009.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Cronan was born in San Francisco, California on June 9, 1951 and grew up near [Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento "Sacramento").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2) As a teenager, he learned [letterpress printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letterpress_printing "Letterpress printing") and had become an artist in a local print shop, creating posters.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)

He studied fine art at [California College of Arts and Crafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_College_of_Arts_and_Crafts "California College of Arts and Crafts") (now known as California College of the Arts) and later graduated from [California State University, Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Sacramento "California State University, Sacramento") (BA degree 1974).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-4) He met his future wife and business partner, Karin Hibma at California State University, Sacramento.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3) Together they had two sons, sculptor and artist, Shawn HibmaCronan; and industrial designer, Nick Cronan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-5)

In 1971, he went abroad to study archeology, and work as an archaeological dig manager for [Hebrew University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_University "Hebrew University") in the [Negev Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negev_Desert "Negev Desert") and then at the [Dead Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea "Dead Sea").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Pacific Wave movement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pacific Wave movement")]

In the early 1980s a few San Francisco–based designers were nicknamed “The Michaels” because they all had the same name (Cronan, alongside [Mabry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Mabry "Michael Mabry"), [Manwaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Manwaring "Michael Manwaring"), [Vanderbyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Vanderbyl "Michael Vanderbyl"), [Schwab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schwab_(designer) "Michael Schwab (designer)")), and later they were known as the "Pacific Wave" according to historian [Steven Heller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Heller_(design_writer) "Steven Heller (design writer)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:3-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-8)

### Cronan Design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cronan Design")]

Cronan and Karin Hibma established Michael Patrick Cronan Design (also known as Cronan Design, but later known simply as Cronan) in 1980.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:2-9) Cronan Design clients including [TiVo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TiVo "TiVo"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)[Kindle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindle_Store "Kindle Store"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10) Good Belly,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)[Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:5-11)[Levi Strauss & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi_Strauss_&_Co. "Levi Strauss & Co."),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:5-11)[Estee Lauder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A9e_Lauder_Companies "Estée Lauder Companies"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:5-11) among others. Cronan Design often worked on [brand-strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_management "Brand management") consulting, they would extensively interview clients and Cronan found naming inspiration by playing with _[Scrabble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrabble "Scrabble")_ tiles for unique letter combinations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:6-1)

In June 2009, he and Karin Hibma were named as two of [Fast Company's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Company_(magazine) "Fast Company (magazine)") list of 100 Most Creative People in Business.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-12)

### Walking Man

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Walking Man")]

Together Cronan and Hibma formed a sub-brand of clothing design, Walking Man, in 1989.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:2-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-13) In 1992 and 1993, Walking Man clothing won the [I.D. Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.D._(magazine) "I.D. (magazine)") Consumer Product of the Year/Gold Award presented at the [Cooper Hewitt National Design Museum, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper-Hewitt,_National_Design_Museum "Cooper-Hewitt, National Design Museum").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Other design experiences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Other design experiences")]

He was an [adjunct professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjunct_professor "Adjunct professor") of graphic design at California College of the Arts from 1981–2001.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Cronan designed the stamp commemorating the fiftieth anniversary of NATO and later the Prostate Awareness stamp for the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service").[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_][[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:4-10)

In 1998, SFMOMA commissioned Cronan to create the SFMOMA symbol which graphically captures the distinctive oculus at the center of the museum building designed by [Mario Botta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Botta "Mario Botta").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Alongside his design work, Cronan had worked as a fine art painter for most of his life.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-14)

His graphic design work is included in many public museum collections including at the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Art "Los Angeles County Museum of Art") (LACMA),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-15) San Francisco Museum of Modern Art,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-16) the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-17) among others.

## Membership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Membership")]

Cronan was a founding member of the [American Institute of Graphic Art (AIGA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA "AIGA") chapter in San Francisco[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:1-3) and the AIGASF chapter president after serving on the AIGA national board for three years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Cronan was Chairman of the Board of the [Pickle Family Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickle_Family_Circus "Pickle Family Circus"), attended the Aspen Leadership Summit in 2005 and served on the Board of the Aspen Design Summit from 2005 – 2006.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Patrick_Cronan&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

*   1985 – _[Pacific Wave](http://designarchives.aiga.org/#/entries/Pacific%20Wave%20Museo%3A%20Fortuny/\_/detail/relevance/asc/0/7/5029/pacific-wave-museo-fortuny/1)_, curated by Giorgio Camuffo, at [Museo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortuny_Museum "Fortuny Museum"), [Venice, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice,_Italy "Venice, Italy")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-:3-6)
*   1993 – _In the Public Eye: The Work of Four Graphic Designers_, [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art") (SFMOMA), San Francisco, California. This exhibition was including Michael Manwaring, [Gerald Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Reis?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gerald Reis (page does not exist)"), and [Michael Vanderbyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Vanderbyl "Michael Vanderbyl"). It was the first graphic design exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and its popularity ushered in an expanded presence of graphics in the museum's floor space and permanent collection.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   2002 – _US Design: 1975-2000_, curated by R. Craig Miller, [Denver Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Art_Museum "Denver Art Museum"), Denver, Colorado[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Patrick_Cronan#cite_note-18)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American graphic artist (born 1943)

| Archie Boston Jr. |
| --- |
| Born | 1943 (age 82–83) Clewiston, Florida, U.S. |
| Occupations | [Graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design"), design educator |
| Awards | [AIGA Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_Medal "AIGA Medal") (2021) |

**Archie Boston Jr.** (born 1943) is an American [graphic artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_designer "Graphic designer"), and retired professor.

Born to an impoverished family in a small town in southern Florida,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) Boston received an education in graphic design[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) at [Chouinard Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouinard_Art_Institute "Chouinard Art Institute") located in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) During school and after graduation, he worked in numerous [ad agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising_agency "Advertising agency") based in Los Angeles[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) before forming Boston & Boston Design with his brother Bradford in 1967—one of the first Black-owned agencies in the United States.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 1972, at age 29, he became the president of the Art Director Club of Los Angeles, the second-largest in the nation. He was the first Black president in the organization's 28-year history.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2)

In 1977 Boston received a master's degree from the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California"), and began his long career as an educator[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4) at [California State University, Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Long_Beach "California State University, Long Beach").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) He helped found the Visual Communications Design program there and served as the department chair.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 2004 he was named Outstanding Professor of the Year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Eye_on_Design-2021-5)

He has produced several documentary films, including _20 Outstanding Los Angeles Designers_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) and, in 2018 with his brother David, he produced the documentary, _Black Pioneers of the Sunshine City_ about the activist members of the Black community in St. Petersburg, Florida[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-WFLA-2018-6)

In 2021, Boston became an American Institute of Graphic Arts medalist.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-2-7)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Born in 1943 in [Clewiston, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clewiston,_Florida "Clewiston, Florida"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) Boston's father was either a [sugar cane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarcane "Sugarcane")[sharecropper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharecropping "Sharecropping") or a migrant worker tilling the sugarcane fields and later became a [truck driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truck_driver "Truck driver").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) His mother raised five children, including Archie, and worked as a [babysitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babysitting "Babysitting").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) The same year as Archie was born, the impoverished family[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) moved to the "Peppertown" area of [St. Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg,_Florida "St. Petersburg, Florida"), a black community of around 14,000 residents occupying about 2 square miles.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) The Boston family may have moved to the Gas Plant area of the community at some point in the 1940s,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) an area that is currently known as Midtown.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-9) Boston graduated from [Gibbs High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs_High_School_(St._Petersburg,_Florida) "Gibbs High School (St. Petersburg, Florida)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)

In 1961, Boston followed in the footsteps of his older brother, Bradford, attending Chouinard Art Institute in Los Angeles (which later became [California Institute of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Institute_of_the_Arts "California Institute of the Arts")).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) National Defense Student Loans funded his education[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) for the first three years and then a [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") Foundation Scholarship funded his final year of graphic design studies.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) He was taught by [Louis Danziger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Danziger "Louis Danziger"), Ken Parkhurst, and Marvin Rubin, graduating with honors in 1965.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 1977 he received his [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") in liberal arts from the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

During his senior year at Chouinard, Boston worked as an [intern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internship "Internship") at the Los Angeles-based advertising agency Carson/Roberts, one of the largest in the West.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-10) He went on to work at various studios, including Hixson and Jorgensen Advertising in 1965, and in 1966 he became an art director at Botsford Ketchum.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 1967, he and his older brother, Bradford, formed Boston & Boston Design, one of the first Black-owned agencies in the United States.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) The two had worked together previously in 1963 producing a series of posters for the Council on Negro Affairs. Boston & Boston Design's clients included Beckman Instruments, [Chiat/Day Advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiat/Day "Chiat/Day"), and Concord Electronics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

In 1969, after two years working together, Archie left Boston & Boston Design, wanting to return to advertising agency work where he would be able to see his concepts realized through published ads.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) He took a position at his previous employer, Carson/Roberts, but shortly after rejoined Botsford Ketchum, where he remained until 1977.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) At Botsford Ketchum, Boston worked on campaigns for [Motorola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola "Motorola"), [Raytheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytheon "Raytheon"), [Yamaha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_Motor_Company "Yamaha Motor Company"), and [Pentel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentel "Pentel"), rounding out his advertising skills with copywriting, notably writing the headline for a Pentel ad, "I told Pentel what to do with their pens. And they did it."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) He also started Archie Boston Graphic Design, an advertising and design consultancy, taking on clients beginning in 1973.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

In 1972, at age 29, Boston became the president of the Art Director Club of Los Angeles, the second-largest in the nation, and was the first black president in the organization's 28-year history.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2)

### Design educator

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design educator")]

Boston first began teaching when he was 23 at Chouinard Art Institute.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) After receiving his master's degree from the University of Southern California in 1977,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4) he began a 32-year-long stint as a full lecturer in the Department of Art at [California State University, Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Long_Beach "California State University, Long Beach").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) In 1978 he helped to found the design department that later became the Visual Communications Design program.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) During his time at [Cal State Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Long_Beach "California State University, Long Beach"), he served 12 terms as the department chair.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) He retired from teaching in 2009.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

## Impact and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Impact and legacy")]

During his first sabbatical at California State University Long Beach, Boston realized the documentary, _20 Outstanding Los Angeles Designers_. For this film, he interviewed leading Los Angeles designers including [Saul Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Bass "Saul Bass"), [Marion Sampler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Sampler "Marion Sampler"), Robert Miles Runyan,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)[Louis Danziger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Danziger "Louis Danziger"), [April Greiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Greiman "April Greiman"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-calarts.on.worldcat.org-11) among other designers. The proceeds from the resulting documentary funded a scholarship for design students in need.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-calarts.on.worldcat.org-11)

In 2018, with his brother David, he co-produced and served as creative director on the documentary, _Black Pioneers of the Sunshine City._ The film chronicles the pioneering work of activist members of the Black community members in St. Petersburg, Florida[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-WFLA-2018-6)

## Recognitions and accomplishments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognitions and accomplishments")]

*   1972 First African American president of the Art Directors Club of Los Angeles, where he served two terms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2)
*   2004 California State University names Boston Outstanding Professor of the Year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Eye_on_Design-2021-5)
*   2007 AIGA Fellows Award, L.A. Chapter of AIGA[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-12)
*   2017 Boston and his work were featured in episode 4[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-13) of the multi-part series _The Real Mad Men of Advertising_[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Eye_on_Design-2021-5)
*   2021 AIGA Medalist[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-2-7)
*   _Graphic Design: USA_ named him as one of 35 design pioneers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)
*   Awarded for his work in [Art Directors Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club_of_New_York "Art Directors Club of New York") Shows including New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)
*   In 2018, [Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University "Duke University") acquired Boston's entire body of work dating from 1963.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American graphic artist (born 1943)

| Archie Boston Jr. |
| --- |
| Born | 1943 (age 82–83) Clewiston, Florida, U.S. |
| Occupations | [Graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design"), design educator |
| Awards | [AIGA Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_Medal "AIGA Medal") (2021) |

**Archie Boston Jr.** (born 1943) is an American [graphic artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_designer "Graphic designer"), and retired professor.

Born to an impoverished family in a small town in southern Florida,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) Boston received an education in graphic design[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) at [Chouinard Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouinard_Art_Institute "Chouinard Art Institute") located in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) During school and after graduation, he worked in numerous [ad agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising_agency "Advertising agency") based in Los Angeles[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) before forming Boston & Boston Design with his brother Bradford in 1967—one of the first Black-owned agencies in the United States.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 1972, at age 29, he became the president of the Art Director Club of Los Angeles, the second-largest in the nation. He was the first Black president in the organization's 28-year history.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2)

In 1977 Boston received a master's degree from the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California"), and began his long career as an educator[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4) at [California State University, Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Long_Beach "California State University, Long Beach").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) He helped found the Visual Communications Design program there and served as the department chair.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 2004 he was named Outstanding Professor of the Year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Eye_on_Design-2021-5)

He has produced several documentary films, including _20 Outstanding Los Angeles Designers_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) and, in 2018 with his brother David, he produced the documentary, _Black Pioneers of the Sunshine City_ about the activist members of the Black community in St. Petersburg, Florida[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-WFLA-2018-6)

In 2021, Boston became an American Institute of Graphic Arts medalist.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-2-7)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Born in 1943 in [Clewiston, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clewiston,_Florida "Clewiston, Florida"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) Boston's father was either a [sugar cane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarcane "Sugarcane")[sharecropper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharecropping "Sharecropping") or a migrant worker tilling the sugarcane fields and later became a [truck driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truck_driver "Truck driver").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) His mother raised five children, including Archie, and worked as a [babysitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babysitting "Babysitting").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) The same year as Archie was born, the impoverished family[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) moved to the "Peppertown" area of [St. Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg,_Florida "St. Petersburg, Florida"), a black community of around 14,000 residents occupying about 2 square miles.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) The Boston family may have moved to the Gas Plant area of the community at some point in the 1940s,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8) an area that is currently known as Midtown.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-9) Boston graduated from [Gibbs High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs_High_School_(St._Petersburg,_Florida) "Gibbs High School (St. Petersburg, Florida)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Donovan-2018-8)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)

In 1961, Boston followed in the footsteps of his older brother, Bradford, attending Chouinard Art Institute in Los Angeles (which later became [California Institute of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Institute_of_the_Arts "California Institute of the Arts")).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) National Defense Student Loans funded his education[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) for the first three years and then a [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") Foundation Scholarship funded his final year of graphic design studies.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) He was taught by [Louis Danziger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Danziger "Louis Danziger"), Ken Parkhurst, and Marvin Rubin, graduating with honors in 1965.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 1977 he received his [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") in liberal arts from the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

During his senior year at Chouinard, Boston worked as an [intern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internship "Internship") at the Los Angeles-based advertising agency Carson/Roberts, one of the largest in the West.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-10) He went on to work at various studios, including Hixson and Jorgensen Advertising in 1965, and in 1966 he became an art director at Botsford Ketchum.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) In 1967, he and his older brother, Bradford, formed Boston & Boston Design, one of the first Black-owned agencies in the United States.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) The two had worked together previously in 1963 producing a series of posters for the Council on Negro Affairs. Boston & Boston Design's clients included Beckman Instruments, [Chiat/Day Advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiat/Day "Chiat/Day"), and Concord Electronics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

In 1969, after two years working together, Archie left Boston & Boston Design, wanting to return to advertising agency work where he would be able to see his concepts realized through published ads.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2) He took a position at his previous employer, Carson/Roberts, but shortly after rejoined Botsford Ketchum, where he remained until 1977.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) At Botsford Ketchum, Boston worked on campaigns for [Motorola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola "Motorola"), [Raytheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytheon "Raytheon"), [Yamaha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_Motor_Company "Yamaha Motor Company"), and [Pentel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentel "Pentel"), rounding out his advertising skills with copywriting, notably writing the headline for a Pentel ad, "I told Pentel what to do with their pens. And they did it."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) He also started Archie Boston Graphic Design, an advertising and design consultancy, taking on clients beginning in 1973.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

In 1972, at age 29, Boston became the president of the Art Director Club of Los Angeles, the second-largest in the nation, and was the first black president in the organization's 28-year history.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2)

### Design educator

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design educator")]

Boston first began teaching when he was 23 at Chouinard Art Institute.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) After receiving his master's degree from the University of Southern California in 1977,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4) he began a 32-year-long stint as a full lecturer in the Department of Art at [California State University, Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Long_Beach "California State University, Long Beach").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) In 1978 he helped to found the design department that later became the Visual Communications Design program.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1) During his time at [Cal State Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Long_Beach "California State University, Long Beach"), he served 12 terms as the department chair.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rapp-2008-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3) He retired from teaching in 2009.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

## Impact and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Impact and legacy")]

During his first sabbatical at California State University Long Beach, Boston realized the documentary, _20 Outstanding Los Angeles Designers_. For this film, he interviewed leading Los Angeles designers including [Saul Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Bass "Saul Bass"), [Marion Sampler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Sampler "Marion Sampler"), Robert Miles Runyan,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)[Louis Danziger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Danziger "Louis Danziger"), [April Greiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Greiman "April Greiman"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-calarts.on.worldcat.org-11) among other designers. The proceeds from the resulting documentary funded a scholarship for design students in need.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-calarts.on.worldcat.org-11)

In 2018, with his brother David, he co-produced and served as creative director on the documentary, _Black Pioneers of the Sunshine City._ The film chronicles the pioneering work of activist members of the Black community members in St. Petersburg, Florida[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-WFLA-2018-6)

## Recognitions and accomplishments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archie_Boston_Jr.&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognitions and accomplishments")]

*   1972 First African American president of the Art Directors Club of Los Angeles, where he served two terms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Rubenstein_Rare_Book-4)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Tampa_Bay_Times-1972-2)
*   2004 California State University names Boston Outstanding Professor of the Year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Eye_on_Design-2021-5)
*   2007 AIGA Fellows Award, L.A. Chapter of AIGA[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-12)
*   2017 Boston and his work were featured in episode 4[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-13) of the multi-part series _The Real Mad Men of Advertising_[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-Eye_on_Design-2021-5)
*   2021 AIGA Medalist[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-2-7)
*   _Graphic Design: USA_ named him as one of 35 design pioneers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)
*   Awarded for his work in [Art Directors Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club_of_New_York "Art Directors Club of New York") Shows including New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)
*   In 2018, [Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University "Duke University") acquired Boston's entire body of work dating from 1963.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Boston_Jr.#cite_note-AIGA-3)

Award

| American Institute of Graphic Arts medal |
| --- |
| [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a7/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts_medal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts_medal.jpg) The physical medal was designed by sculptor [James Earle Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Earle_Fraser_(sculptor) "James Earle Fraser (sculptor)") in 1920.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_Medal#cite_note-1) |
| Awarded for | Exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication") |
| Presented by | [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) |
| First award | 1920;106 years ago(1920) |
| Website | [www.aiga.org](http://www.aiga.org/) |

Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_Medal#cite_note-2) the [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication")."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_Medal#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.

Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_Medal#cite_note-2) the [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication")."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_Medal#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.

Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

**Alexander Girard** (May 24, 1907 – December 31, 1993) was an architect, interior designer, furniture designer, industrial designer, and a [textile designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_design "Textile design").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-2)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born in New York City to an American mother from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") and a French-Italian father. He was raised in [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), Italy and in 1917, he was sent as a boarder to [Bedford Modern School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford_Modern_School "Bedford Modern School") in England leaving in 1924 to study architecture in London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-5) After also graduating from the Royal School of Architecture in Rome, Girard refined his skills in both Florence and New York. In 1932, his studio was opened in New York and he moved it to [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit") in 1937.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/La_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_Alexander_Girard%2C_1960.jpg/250px-La_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_Alexander_Girard%2C_1960.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:La_Fonda_Del_Sol,_Alexander_Girard,_1960.jpg)

_La Fonda Del Sol_ by Girard (1960)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Peinture_de_soleil%2C_explorations_pour_la_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_1960.jpg/250px-Peinture_de_soleil%2C_explorations_pour_la_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_1960.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peinture_de_soleil,_explorations_pour_la_Fonda_Del_Sol,_1960.jpg)

Colour studies for _La Fonda Del Sol_

Girard is widely known for his contributions in the field of American [textile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile "Textile") design, particularly through his work for [Herman Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Miller_(manufacturer) "Herman Miller (manufacturer)") (1952 to 1973), where he created fabrics for the designs of [George Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nelson_(designer) "George Nelson (designer)") and [Charles and Ray Eames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_and_Ray_Eames "Charles and Ray Eames").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-7)

His work also includes designing the La Fonda del Sol Restaurant in New York (1960), the Herman Miller Showplace: T&O (Textiles and Objects) (1961), [Braniff International Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braniff_International_Airways "Braniff International Airways") (1965), and the Girard Foundation (1962), which houses his extensive [folk art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_art "Folk art") collection. He and his wife, Susan Girard, amassed a remarkable collection of artifacts consisting of folk art, popular art, toys, and textiles from around the world, which is displayed through the Girard Foundation, founded 1962. One of the artists Girard supported was [Cochiti Pueblo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochiti_Pueblo "Cochiti Pueblo")[potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pottery "Pottery")[Helen Cordero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Cordero "Helen Cordero"), the creator of [Storyteller pottery figurines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storyteller_(pottery) "Storyteller (pottery)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-8)

Girard died from complications of Alzheimer's disease at his home in Santa Fe on December 31, 1993.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-9)

## Girard at Herman Miller

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Girard at Herman Miller")]

### Herman Miller Textiles Division

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Herman Miller Textiles Division")]

In 1952, Alexander Girard was hired to head the fabric and textile division.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Girard worked with [George Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nelson_(designer) "George Nelson (designer)") and Charles and Ray Eames to form a design team that has influenced the fundamentals of design throughout the United States and the rest of the world. Girard initially established a fabric collection based on his architectural training.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) His first fabric line consisted of plain upholsteries and geometric drapery prints—stripes, circles, and triangles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) He went on to create many more patterns and designs, largely inspired by folk art.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) He also worked with a [textile mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_mill "Textile mill"), Telares Uruapan, which he discovered in central Mexico, to create a line of handwoven 100% cotton fabrics.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Because of the excellent quality and array of colors available, he developed a range of colorful "mexidots"and "mexistripes" which he used in many of his projects including installation backing, ground for environmental enrichment panels and upholstery.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10)

Girard also developed a furniture collection for [Herman Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Miller_(manufacturer) "Herman Miller (manufacturer)") in 1967 building on his designs for [Braniff Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braniff_Airlines "Braniff Airlines")' lounge and office furniture which featured a low sight line and interior/exterior shell separate from the seat cushion to maximize varied upholstery.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Originals from this collection are rare and have become highly collectible, since they were quite expensive at the time and were in production only for one year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) In 1971, he developed 40 screen printed graphics on fabrics for Robert Propst's Action Office 2 System.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) These Environmental Enrichment panels add a touch of warmth, color, and design to the office environment.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10)

### T&O (Textiles and Objects) 1961

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: T&O (Textiles and Objects) 1961")]

This Herman Miller showplace was a unique space filled with textiles and folk art pieces on Manhattan's East 53rd Street.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Textiles and Objects was an innovation demonstrating textiles as an integral part of interior displays for both designers and the individual consumer.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) The showroom also featured folk art Girard collected from around the world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) T&O closed in shortly after opening, due to insufficient marketing and a public was not quite ready to add such colorful and exotic objects to the typical 1950s, palette of their homes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10)

## Independent projects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Independent projects")]

### Braniff Airways and "The End of The Plain Plane"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Braniff Airways and \"The End of The Plain Plane\"")]

In May 1965, Girard began his design work for [Braniff International Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braniff_International_Airways "Braniff International Airways") re-branding campaign called "The End of the Plain Plane". This project gave Girard the opportunity to work with textiles, color, and graphics on a grand scale, redesigning everything from the sugar packets to the ticket counters to the color of the planes themselves. He used colors like light and dark blue, beige, ochre, orange, turquoise, and lemon yellow to make the planes recognizable from the ground. Italian couturier fashion designer [Emilio Pucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Pucci "Emilio Pucci") designed attendant uniforms.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-Nance-11)

Girard also designed a line of furniture for Braniff's ticket offices and customer lounges. This furniture was also available to the public by Herman Miller in 1967, but was available for one year only.

### Restaurants

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Restaurants")]

In 1960, Girard designed every aspect of the La Fonda del Sol restaurant located in Manhattan's Time-Life building in a Latin American and contemporary theme/style, including menus, matchbooks, tableware and the ceramic tiles on the floors and walls. Girard created over eighty different sun motifs found throughout the restaurant.

As part of the commission, Charles and Ray Eames were brought in to design a fabric covered fiberglass chair and table, both with a new pedestal design. The chairs were similar to the plastic Eames chairs with a modification to the top silhouette of the fiberglass bucket.

Girard was also commissioned by Brody to design the L'Etoile Restaurant (1966) in the Sherry Netherlands Hotel, New York, a French restaurant with austere decor featuring a range of silver and greys featuring glass engraved with the names of French luminaries and daisy shaped tables in the bar.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-12) The Compound Restaurant (1967), in Santa Fe, New Mexico, is in a clean modern yet traditional New Mexican style with inlaid Mexicotton ceiling tiles and nichos featuring a mix of folk art and Girard's own designs.

### Georg Jensen

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Georg Jensen")]

In 1956, Just Lunning, president of Georg Jensen, commissioned Girard to design seven table settings for an exhibition on 5th Avenue in New York. Each setting was created around a vignette outlining the personalities and situations of the company at the particular table. He created place mats and dishes specific to the project.

### John Deere

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: John Deere")]

Girard was commissioned to create a mural for the [John Deere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Deere "John Deere") Company, in the entrance to their administration building designed by Eero Saarinen near Moline, Illinois. The mural is one hundred eighty feet long and eight feet high, created entirely with three dimensional found objects.

### The Girard Foundation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: The Girard Foundation")]

In 1962, Girard and his wife established the Girard Foundation in Santa Fe to manage their art collection that numbered over 100,000 pieces, including toys, dolls, icons, and other ethnic expressions. Girard's design work was heavily influenced by his passion for folk art. In 1978, Girard contributed his immense collection to the [Museum of International Folk Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_International_Folk_Art "Museum of International Folk Art") in [Santa Fe, New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe,_New_Mexico "Santa Fe, New Mexico"), United States. The museum opened to the public in 1953, and has gained national and international recognition as home to the world's largest collection of folk art.

The [Girard Wing](https://web.archive.org/web/20070621065532/http://www.internationalfolkart.org/about/girard.html) houses the popular permanent exhibition, _Multiple Visions: A Common Bond_, which showcases folk art, popular art, toys and textiles from more than 100 nations. Opening in 1982, this unorthodox exhibition was designed and installed by Girard, and remains popular with the public.

## Wooden Dolls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Wooden Dolls")]

Girard designed the Wooden Dolls in 1952.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-Vitra-16) The Wooden Dolls were used for his Santa Fe home.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-Vitra-16) They were human and animal characters with various colors. After Girard's heirs donated it to the Vitra Design Museum, it was studied and imitated and produced.

## Typography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Typography")]

Girard designed his own typeface and used it in other design works through typography.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-17) The fonts he designed are practical, illustrative and readable.
