**Alexander Girard** (May 24, 1907 – December 31, 1993) was an architect, interior designer, furniture designer, industrial designer, and a [textile designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_design "Textile design").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-2)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born in New York City to an American mother from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") and a French-Italian father. He was raised in [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), Italy and in 1917, he was sent as a boarder to [Bedford Modern School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford_Modern_School "Bedford Modern School") in England leaving in 1924 to study architecture in London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-5) After also graduating from the Royal School of Architecture in Rome, Girard refined his skills in both Florence and New York. In 1932, his studio was opened in New York and he moved it to [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit") in 1937.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/La_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_Alexander_Girard%2C_1960.jpg/250px-La_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_Alexander_Girard%2C_1960.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:La_Fonda_Del_Sol,_Alexander_Girard,_1960.jpg)

_La Fonda Del Sol_ by Girard (1960)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Peinture_de_soleil%2C_explorations_pour_la_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_1960.jpg/250px-Peinture_de_soleil%2C_explorations_pour_la_Fonda_Del_Sol%2C_1960.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peinture_de_soleil,_explorations_pour_la_Fonda_Del_Sol,_1960.jpg)

Colour studies for _La Fonda Del Sol_

Girard is widely known for his contributions in the field of American [textile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile "Textile") design, particularly through his work for [Herman Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Miller_(manufacturer) "Herman Miller (manufacturer)") (1952 to 1973), where he created fabrics for the designs of [George Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nelson_(designer) "George Nelson (designer)") and [Charles and Ray Eames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_and_Ray_Eames "Charles and Ray Eames").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-7)

His work also includes designing the La Fonda del Sol Restaurant in New York (1960), the Herman Miller Showplace: T&O (Textiles and Objects) (1961), [Braniff International Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braniff_International_Airways "Braniff International Airways") (1965), and the Girard Foundation (1962), which houses his extensive [folk art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_art "Folk art") collection. He and his wife, Susan Girard, amassed a remarkable collection of artifacts consisting of folk art, popular art, toys, and textiles from around the world, which is displayed through the Girard Foundation, founded 1962. One of the artists Girard supported was [Cochiti Pueblo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochiti_Pueblo "Cochiti Pueblo")[potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pottery "Pottery")[Helen Cordero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Cordero "Helen Cordero"), the creator of [Storyteller pottery figurines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storyteller_(pottery) "Storyteller (pottery)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-8)

Girard died from complications of Alzheimer's disease at his home in Santa Fe on December 31, 1993.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-9)

## Girard at Herman Miller

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Girard at Herman Miller")]

### Herman Miller Textiles Division

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Herman Miller Textiles Division")]

In 1952, Alexander Girard was hired to head the fabric and textile division.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Girard worked with [George Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nelson_(designer) "George Nelson (designer)") and Charles and Ray Eames to form a design team that has influenced the fundamentals of design throughout the United States and the rest of the world. Girard initially established a fabric collection based on his architectural training.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) His first fabric line consisted of plain upholsteries and geometric drapery prints—stripes, circles, and triangles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) He went on to create many more patterns and designs, largely inspired by folk art.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) He also worked with a [textile mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_mill "Textile mill"), Telares Uruapan, which he discovered in central Mexico, to create a line of handwoven 100% cotton fabrics.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Because of the excellent quality and array of colors available, he developed a range of colorful "mexidots"and "mexistripes" which he used in many of his projects including installation backing, ground for environmental enrichment panels and upholstery.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10)

Girard also developed a furniture collection for [Herman Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Miller_(manufacturer) "Herman Miller (manufacturer)") in 1967 building on his designs for [Braniff Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braniff_Airlines "Braniff Airlines")' lounge and office furniture which featured a low sight line and interior/exterior shell separate from the seat cushion to maximize varied upholstery.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Originals from this collection are rare and have become highly collectible, since they were quite expensive at the time and were in production only for one year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) In 1971, he developed 40 screen printed graphics on fabrics for Robert Propst's Action Office 2 System.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) These Environmental Enrichment panels add a touch of warmth, color, and design to the office environment.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10)

### T&O (Textiles and Objects) 1961

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: T&O (Textiles and Objects) 1961")]

This Herman Miller showplace was a unique space filled with textiles and folk art pieces on Manhattan's East 53rd Street.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) Textiles and Objects was an innovation demonstrating textiles as an integral part of interior displays for both designers and the individual consumer.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) The showroom also featured folk art Girard collected from around the world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10) T&O closed in shortly after opening, due to insufficient marketing and a public was not quite ready to add such colorful and exotic objects to the typical 1950s, palette of their homes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-hermanmiller.com-10)

## Independent projects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Independent projects")]

### Braniff Airways and "The End of The Plain Plane"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Braniff Airways and \"The End of The Plain Plane\"")]

In May 1965, Girard began his design work for [Braniff International Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braniff_International_Airways "Braniff International Airways") re-branding campaign called "The End of the Plain Plane". This project gave Girard the opportunity to work with textiles, color, and graphics on a grand scale, redesigning everything from the sugar packets to the ticket counters to the color of the planes themselves. He used colors like light and dark blue, beige, ochre, orange, turquoise, and lemon yellow to make the planes recognizable from the ground. Italian couturier fashion designer [Emilio Pucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Pucci "Emilio Pucci") designed attendant uniforms.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-Nance-11)

Girard also designed a line of furniture for Braniff's ticket offices and customer lounges. This furniture was also available to the public by Herman Miller in 1967, but was available for one year only.

### Restaurants

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Restaurants")]

In 1960, Girard designed every aspect of the La Fonda del Sol restaurant located in Manhattan's Time-Life building in a Latin American and contemporary theme/style, including menus, matchbooks, tableware and the ceramic tiles on the floors and walls. Girard created over eighty different sun motifs found throughout the restaurant.

As part of the commission, Charles and Ray Eames were brought in to design a fabric covered fiberglass chair and table, both with a new pedestal design. The chairs were similar to the plastic Eames chairs with a modification to the top silhouette of the fiberglass bucket.

Girard was also commissioned by Brody to design the L'Etoile Restaurant (1966) in the Sherry Netherlands Hotel, New York, a French restaurant with austere decor featuring a range of silver and greys featuring glass engraved with the names of French luminaries and daisy shaped tables in the bar.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-12) The Compound Restaurant (1967), in Santa Fe, New Mexico, is in a clean modern yet traditional New Mexican style with inlaid Mexicotton ceiling tiles and nichos featuring a mix of folk art and Girard's own designs.

### Georg Jensen

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Georg Jensen")]

In 1956, Just Lunning, president of Georg Jensen, commissioned Girard to design seven table settings for an exhibition on 5th Avenue in New York. Each setting was created around a vignette outlining the personalities and situations of the company at the particular table. He created place mats and dishes specific to the project.

### John Deere

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: John Deere")]

Girard was commissioned to create a mural for the [John Deere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Deere "John Deere") Company, in the entrance to their administration building designed by Eero Saarinen near Moline, Illinois. The mural is one hundred eighty feet long and eight feet high, created entirely with three dimensional found objects.

### The Girard Foundation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: The Girard Foundation")]

In 1962, Girard and his wife established the Girard Foundation in Santa Fe to manage their art collection that numbered over 100,000 pieces, including toys, dolls, icons, and other ethnic expressions. Girard's design work was heavily influenced by his passion for folk art. In 1978, Girard contributed his immense collection to the [Museum of International Folk Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_International_Folk_Art "Museum of International Folk Art") in [Santa Fe, New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe,_New_Mexico "Santa Fe, New Mexico"), United States. The museum opened to the public in 1953, and has gained national and international recognition as home to the world's largest collection of folk art.

The [Girard Wing](https://web.archive.org/web/20070621065532/http://www.internationalfolkart.org/about/girard.html) houses the popular permanent exhibition, _Multiple Visions: A Common Bond_, which showcases folk art, popular art, toys and textiles from more than 100 nations. Opening in 1982, this unorthodox exhibition was designed and installed by Girard, and remains popular with the public.

## Wooden Dolls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Wooden Dolls")]

Girard designed the Wooden Dolls in 1952.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-Vitra-16) The Wooden Dolls were used for his Santa Fe home.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-Vitra-16) They were human and animal characters with various colors. After Girard's heirs donated it to the Vitra Design Museum, it was studied and imitated and produced.

## Typography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Girard&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Typography")]

Girard designed his own typeface and used it in other design works through typography.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Girard#cite_note-17) The fonts he designed are practical, illustrative and readable.

**Thomas Miller** (December 24, 1920 – July 19, 2012)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-hm2-1) was an American [graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_arts "Visual arts"), whose best known publicly accessible work is the collection of mosaics of the founders of [DuSable Museum of African American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuSable_Museum_of_African_American_History "DuSable Museum of African American History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"). He designed the logos of [Motorola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola "Motorola") and the [Peace Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Corps "Peace Corps") while employed at the Chicago studio of [Morton Goldsholl Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Goldsholl_Associates "Morton Goldsholl Associates") and was the creative director of the 1975 rebrand of [7-Up.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_Up "7 Up")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-2)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

Miller was born in [Bristol, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol,_Virginia "Bristol, Virginia"), where he graduated from Douglas High School in 1937. He then attended [Virginia State College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_State_College "Virginia State College") (now Virginia State University) which was founded in 1882 as the country's first fully state supported four-year institution of higher learning for [African-Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American").

He graduated from there in 1941 after having earned a bachelor's degree in education with a focus on art, and subsequently enlisted in the U.S. Army, where he attained the rank of first sergeant, serving in the 3437 Quartermaster Truck Company[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-4) during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

### Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Education")]

Although a formal education in art was not available to Miller during his childhood, he pursued his interest with a tenacity that would prove to be a prominent characteristic of his personality later in life. The black libraries that were accessible to him as a child in the south were generally not provided with the art history books that he was interested in studying, but he was able to use libraries normally accessible only to white people to explore the offerings of history's major artists.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-5) It was there that Miller discovered [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-Fitzpatrick_Southland,_p.1-6) whose work was an inspiration that continued to influence him to the end of his life.

Miller didn't have the opportunity to formally study [Commercial art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_art "Commercial art") until he came to Chicago after being discharged from the army.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-margolin-7) It was there, determined to develop his talent, that Miller applied to and was accepted as a student at the Ray Vogue School of Art. This was not easily accomplished in those days, and he and his fellow student Emmett McBain ". . .were the only African-Americans [there] besides the janitors."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-margolin-7) The school had been founded in 1916 as The Commercial Art School, and was one of the first colleges of applied art and design in the United States.

By 1946, when Miller became a student, Ray Vogue had a national reputation as a leading educator in professional art and fashion design. While at Ray Vogue, Miller studied commercial and graphic art, and completed his studies there in 1950.

### Morton Goldsholl Associates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Morton Goldsholl Associates")]

Miller began his career as a professional artist with a brief stint in the Chicago offices of Gerstel-Loeff before joining [Morton Goldsholl Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Goldsholl_Associates "Morton Goldsholl Associates"), a studio that was known at the time for its "progressive hiring policies", in that it was one of the few firms then that hired minorities and women in a professional capacity.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-8) Because it was a small office with a reputation for innovation and quality, it was a rare occasion when a chance to work for Goldsholl presented itself, and when this happened in 1950, Miller pursued the opportunity with his usual diligence.

Years later during an interview, he described an early part of the discussion he had with Goldsholl (1911–1995): "Morton Goldsholl told me, unlike the other people, that he wanted a designer. And he said that he wasn't hiring me because I was black and he felt sorry for me. He said he was hiring me because he needed a designer. That turned a corner for me."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-9)

The road to Goldsholl was not an easy one, considering that it was necessary for Miller to overcome the obstacle that was created by the color of his skin. Although armed with a degree from a respected state university and later training as a commercial artist from a prestigious school, it became necessary for Miller to leave his wife Anita and their two children in the care of her sister in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), where the two women taught in the public schools, while he set out to find employment where he would be hired as an equal in his field.

His first efforts were made in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"), and although he received an offer of employment with the understanding that he could work behind a screen so that his presence would not be obvious to the other designers and corporate clients, he considered this circumstance to be unacceptable. After exhausting whatever possibilities might have existed in the [Northeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States "Northeastern United States"), the next stop on his itinerary was Chicago, where he landed a job first with Gerstel-Loeff, and eventually with Morton Goldsholl. Miller flourished there, staying until his retirement some thirty-five years later.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-10)

Although a relatively small firm by Chicago standards (the office was founded in the early 1940s and consisted of only about a dozen people at any given time, including Morton Goldsholl and his wife, [Millie Goldsholl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millie_Goldsholl "Millie Goldsholl")), it was considered to be one of the best on the city of Chicago.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-11) In 1951, the firm was hired to develop the logo and graphic identity for Good Design, a collaborative exhibition and promotional program jointly developed by the Chicago Merchandise Mart and the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") in New York after the success of the 1950 season.

The Goldsholls studied under [László Moholy-Nagy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_Moholy-Nagy "László Moholy-Nagy")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-12) at the [New Bauhaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bauhaus "New Bauhaus") (now the [IIT Institute of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IIT_Institute_of_Design "IIT Institute of Design") at the [Illinois Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Institute_of_Technology "Illinois Institute of Technology")), and as the studio developed, it became internationally renowned for its creative output, which included animation[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-16) and the development of branding and packaging for major international organizations like [Motorola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola "Motorola"), [Quaker Oats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaker_Oats_Company "Quaker Oats Company") and the [Peace Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Corps "Peace Corps").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:1-17) Animation by the firm included commercials for companies the caliber of [Gillette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillette_(brand) "Gillette (brand)") and [Hallmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallmark_Cards "Hallmark Cards"), whose advertising budgets would allow them to go anywhere, but who instead elected to come to Morton Goldsholl Associates, "The most successful of [Chicago] animation producers".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-19) Millie Goldsholl was an accomplished photographer and was one of the founders in 1975 of the Midwest USA Chapter of ASIFA, the [International Animated Film Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Animated_Film_Association "International Animated Film Association") (l'Association Internationale du Film d'Animation).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-20)

The innovation of Morton Goldsholl Associates wasn't expressed only in art _per se_ - for example in 1953 the firm designed "a new line of modern [children's] furniture that was designed to 'grow'" with the child,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-21) and was awarded a patent in 1985 for the invention of an "Image processor and method for use in making photographic prints", which was capable of making unusual images using ordinary photographic film.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-22) During his career at Goldsholl, Miller contributed to many of these projects, and was the primary designer at the studio of the new packaging and identity for [7-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7-up "7-up") in the mid-1970s.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:0-24) "The inspiration for the design just came to me" he said once during and interview. "What better way to represent graphically the [effervescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effervescence "Effervescence") of a carbonated beverage than by using circles as the basis of the design". For this project and others he earned several awards for both himself and for his company.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:0-24)

He was the first African American to break into the mainstream profession of graphic artist, and during the 1950s and 60's was one of few to maintain a membership in traditional trade organizations like The Society of Typographical Arts. Connections such as these were necessary to maintain and advance one's career.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:1-17)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-25)

### Freelance work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Freelance work")]

Miller's career as an independent artist began unwittingly during the time he was stationed in Europe during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). With the shortages caused by the war, Miller's media by necessity was whatever he could lay his hands on - proper paper, pencils, paint and chalk were hard to come by[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-hm2-1)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-26) - but never one to pass on an opportunity to paint, draw or sketch, Miller took whatever art paraphernalia he could improvise and went out on his free time to artistically record the beauty that was still Europe. This frequently led to a spontaneous commission, where Miller would part with his current project for pocket change (or equally as often by making a gift of it) when a passer-by stopped to admire his work. After the war and while he worked at Goldsholl Associates, Miller continued as an independent artist both by private commission and by displaying his work at various venues.

#### Founders Memorial at Du Sable Museum Chicago

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Founders Memorial at Du Sable Museum Chicago")]

The founders' murals are Miller's _magnum opus_, and beautifully demonstrate the creativity that is typical of his work. Unlike traditional mosaic that is made with earthenware or glass tile, these are made from thousands of pieces of plastic that were harvested from plastic egg crate light diffusers which were then individually colored and arranged to create the images in the series. "Anybody can do an oil painting," he said during an interview, "but to take a face and do it with squares is hard. They have to be turned at an angle to catch the light".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-Fitzpatrick_Southland,_p.1-6)

In addition to portraits of the founders, the series includes a portrait of [Jean Baptiste Point du Sable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Baptiste_Point_du_Sable "Jean Baptiste Point du Sable"), the late Chicago mayor [Harold Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Washington "Harold Washington"), and a collage depicting the history of Chicago.It was at a show at [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_Chicago "Hyde Park, Chicago") in Chicago that Miller was approached by Margaret Taylor-Burroughs, then director of the DuSable Museum, to create some kind of memorial to the museum's founders. This meeting resulted in the creation of the Thomas Miller mosaics. Miller also used his talents to copy the works of better known artists for collectors who either couldn't afford the originals or which by their very nature were unavailable. For these commissions, the "copies" were always made different in some respect, either by a change in the size or color, or by the addition of some feature which only a side-by-side comparison of the original would reveal. This was an opportunity for Miller to study the style and technique of other artists, and served as an educational experience for him.

## Archive

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Archive")]

The _Thomas H. E. Miller design papers (MSMill99)_ are held at the [University of Illinois Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago "University of Illinois Chicago") archive. The collection includes photographs, proofsheets, slides, award certificates, realia, prototypes, calendars, periodicals and samples of his branding designs ranging from 1953-1996.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-27)

## Later life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Later life and death")]

Miller moved into the Smith Village [assisted living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assisted_living "Assisted living") home in the [Morgan Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Park,_Chicago "Morgan Park, Chicago") community in Chicago, where he continued to paint. The dining room at Smith Village was named after him in 2008 when he was 88 years old. Thomas Miller died in his sleep at his home on July 19, 2012.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-32)

## Awards and recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Awards and recognition")]

In 2021, Miller was posthumously awarded the AIGA Medal for "expanding recognition".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-33)

**Thomas Miller** (December 24, 1920 – July 19, 2012)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-hm2-1) was an American [graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_arts "Visual arts"), whose best known publicly accessible work is the collection of mosaics of the founders of [DuSable Museum of African American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuSable_Museum_of_African_American_History "DuSable Museum of African American History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"). He designed the logos of [Motorola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola "Motorola") and the [Peace Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Corps "Peace Corps") while employed at the Chicago studio of [Morton Goldsholl Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Goldsholl_Associates "Morton Goldsholl Associates") and was the creative director of the 1975 rebrand of [7-Up.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_Up "7 Up")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-2)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

Miller was born in [Bristol, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol,_Virginia "Bristol, Virginia"), where he graduated from Douglas High School in 1937. He then attended [Virginia State College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_State_College "Virginia State College") (now Virginia State University) which was founded in 1882 as the country's first fully state supported four-year institution of higher learning for [African-Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American").

He graduated from there in 1941 after having earned a bachelor's degree in education with a focus on art, and subsequently enlisted in the U.S. Army, where he attained the rank of first sergeant, serving in the 3437 Quartermaster Truck Company[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-4) during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

### Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Education")]

Although a formal education in art was not available to Miller during his childhood, he pursued his interest with a tenacity that would prove to be a prominent characteristic of his personality later in life. The black libraries that were accessible to him as a child in the south were generally not provided with the art history books that he was interested in studying, but he was able to use libraries normally accessible only to white people to explore the offerings of history's major artists.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-5) It was there that Miller discovered [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-Fitzpatrick_Southland,_p.1-6) whose work was an inspiration that continued to influence him to the end of his life.

Miller didn't have the opportunity to formally study [Commercial art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_art "Commercial art") until he came to Chicago after being discharged from the army.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-margolin-7) It was there, determined to develop his talent, that Miller applied to and was accepted as a student at the Ray Vogue School of Art. This was not easily accomplished in those days, and he and his fellow student Emmett McBain ". . .were the only African-Americans [there] besides the janitors."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-margolin-7) The school had been founded in 1916 as The Commercial Art School, and was one of the first colleges of applied art and design in the United States.

By 1946, when Miller became a student, Ray Vogue had a national reputation as a leading educator in professional art and fashion design. While at Ray Vogue, Miller studied commercial and graphic art, and completed his studies there in 1950.

### Morton Goldsholl Associates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Morton Goldsholl Associates")]

Miller began his career as a professional artist with a brief stint in the Chicago offices of Gerstel-Loeff before joining [Morton Goldsholl Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Goldsholl_Associates "Morton Goldsholl Associates"), a studio that was known at the time for its "progressive hiring policies", in that it was one of the few firms then that hired minorities and women in a professional capacity.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-8) Because it was a small office with a reputation for innovation and quality, it was a rare occasion when a chance to work for Goldsholl presented itself, and when this happened in 1950, Miller pursued the opportunity with his usual diligence.

Years later during an interview, he described an early part of the discussion he had with Goldsholl (1911–1995): "Morton Goldsholl told me, unlike the other people, that he wanted a designer. And he said that he wasn't hiring me because I was black and he felt sorry for me. He said he was hiring me because he needed a designer. That turned a corner for me."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-9)

The road to Goldsholl was not an easy one, considering that it was necessary for Miller to overcome the obstacle that was created by the color of his skin. Although armed with a degree from a respected state university and later training as a commercial artist from a prestigious school, it became necessary for Miller to leave his wife Anita and their two children in the care of her sister in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), where the two women taught in the public schools, while he set out to find employment where he would be hired as an equal in his field.

His first efforts were made in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"), and although he received an offer of employment with the understanding that he could work behind a screen so that his presence would not be obvious to the other designers and corporate clients, he considered this circumstance to be unacceptable. After exhausting whatever possibilities might have existed in the [Northeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States "Northeastern United States"), the next stop on his itinerary was Chicago, where he landed a job first with Gerstel-Loeff, and eventually with Morton Goldsholl. Miller flourished there, staying until his retirement some thirty-five years later.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-10)

Although a relatively small firm by Chicago standards (the office was founded in the early 1940s and consisted of only about a dozen people at any given time, including Morton Goldsholl and his wife, [Millie Goldsholl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millie_Goldsholl "Millie Goldsholl")), it was considered to be one of the best on the city of Chicago.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-11) In 1951, the firm was hired to develop the logo and graphic identity for Good Design, a collaborative exhibition and promotional program jointly developed by the Chicago Merchandise Mart and the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") in New York after the success of the 1950 season.

The Goldsholls studied under [László Moholy-Nagy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_Moholy-Nagy "László Moholy-Nagy")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-12) at the [New Bauhaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bauhaus "New Bauhaus") (now the [IIT Institute of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IIT_Institute_of_Design "IIT Institute of Design") at the [Illinois Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Institute_of_Technology "Illinois Institute of Technology")), and as the studio developed, it became internationally renowned for its creative output, which included animation[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-16) and the development of branding and packaging for major international organizations like [Motorola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola "Motorola"), [Quaker Oats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaker_Oats_Company "Quaker Oats Company") and the [Peace Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Corps "Peace Corps").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:1-17) Animation by the firm included commercials for companies the caliber of [Gillette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillette_(brand) "Gillette (brand)") and [Hallmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallmark_Cards "Hallmark Cards"), whose advertising budgets would allow them to go anywhere, but who instead elected to come to Morton Goldsholl Associates, "The most successful of [Chicago] animation producers".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-19) Millie Goldsholl was an accomplished photographer and was one of the founders in 1975 of the Midwest USA Chapter of ASIFA, the [International Animated Film Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Animated_Film_Association "International Animated Film Association") (l'Association Internationale du Film d'Animation).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-20)

The innovation of Morton Goldsholl Associates wasn't expressed only in art _per se_ - for example in 1953 the firm designed "a new line of modern [children's] furniture that was designed to 'grow'" with the child,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-21) and was awarded a patent in 1985 for the invention of an "Image processor and method for use in making photographic prints", which was capable of making unusual images using ordinary photographic film.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-22) During his career at Goldsholl, Miller contributed to many of these projects, and was the primary designer at the studio of the new packaging and identity for [7-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7-up "7-up") in the mid-1970s.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:0-24) "The inspiration for the design just came to me" he said once during and interview. "What better way to represent graphically the [effervescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effervescence "Effervescence") of a carbonated beverage than by using circles as the basis of the design". For this project and others he earned several awards for both himself and for his company.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:0-24)

He was the first African American to break into the mainstream profession of graphic artist, and during the 1950s and 60's was one of few to maintain a membership in traditional trade organizations like The Society of Typographical Arts. Connections such as these were necessary to maintain and advance one's career.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-:1-17)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-25)

### Freelance work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Freelance work")]

Miller's career as an independent artist began unwittingly during the time he was stationed in Europe during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). With the shortages caused by the war, Miller's media by necessity was whatever he could lay his hands on - proper paper, pencils, paint and chalk were hard to come by[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-hm2-1)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-26) - but never one to pass on an opportunity to paint, draw or sketch, Miller took whatever art paraphernalia he could improvise and went out on his free time to artistically record the beauty that was still Europe. This frequently led to a spontaneous commission, where Miller would part with his current project for pocket change (or equally as often by making a gift of it) when a passer-by stopped to admire his work. After the war and while he worked at Goldsholl Associates, Miller continued as an independent artist both by private commission and by displaying his work at various venues.

#### Founders Memorial at Du Sable Museum Chicago

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Founders Memorial at Du Sable Museum Chicago")]

The founders' murals are Miller's _magnum opus_, and beautifully demonstrate the creativity that is typical of his work. Unlike traditional mosaic that is made with earthenware or glass tile, these are made from thousands of pieces of plastic that were harvested from plastic egg crate light diffusers which were then individually colored and arranged to create the images in the series. "Anybody can do an oil painting," he said during an interview, "but to take a face and do it with squares is hard. They have to be turned at an angle to catch the light".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-Fitzpatrick_Southland,_p.1-6)

In addition to portraits of the founders, the series includes a portrait of [Jean Baptiste Point du Sable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Baptiste_Point_du_Sable "Jean Baptiste Point du Sable"), the late Chicago mayor [Harold Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Washington "Harold Washington"), and a collage depicting the history of Chicago.It was at a show at [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_Chicago "Hyde Park, Chicago") in Chicago that Miller was approached by Margaret Taylor-Burroughs, then director of the DuSable Museum, to create some kind of memorial to the museum's founders. This meeting resulted in the creation of the Thomas Miller mosaics. Miller also used his talents to copy the works of better known artists for collectors who either couldn't afford the originals or which by their very nature were unavailable. For these commissions, the "copies" were always made different in some respect, either by a change in the size or color, or by the addition of some feature which only a side-by-side comparison of the original would reveal. This was an opportunity for Miller to study the style and technique of other artists, and served as an educational experience for him.

## Archive

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Archive")]

The _Thomas H. E. Miller design papers (MSMill99)_ are held at the [University of Illinois Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago "University of Illinois Chicago") archive. The collection includes photographs, proofsheets, slides, award certificates, realia, prototypes, calendars, periodicals and samples of his branding designs ranging from 1953-1996.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-27)

## Later life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Later life and death")]

Miller moved into the Smith Village [assisted living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assisted_living "Assisted living") home in the [Morgan Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Park,_Chicago "Morgan Park, Chicago") community in Chicago, where he continued to paint. The dining room at Smith Village was named after him in 2008 when he was 88 years old. Thomas Miller died in his sleep at his home on July 19, 2012.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-32)

## Awards and recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Awards and recognition")]

In 2021, Miller was posthumously awarded the AIGA Medal for "expanding recognition".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-33)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Television director

**Karin Fong** is an American [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards")-winning director and designer[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:0-1) based in [Los Angeles, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). She is a co-founder of Imaginary Forces,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-2) a design studio and creative agency best known for its portfolio of work in [main title design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_title_design "Film title design") for [television series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show") and [motion pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_pictures "Motion pictures").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-3) Fong was awarded the 2018 AIGA Medal, the highest distinction in the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") in the U.S., in recognition of her achievements as a [visual storyteller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_narrative "Visual narrative"), [motion graphics designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_graphic_design "Motion graphic design"), and director.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:3-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-5)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Karin_Fong&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Fong was born in 1971 in [Canoga Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoga_Park,_Los_Angeles "Canoga Park, Los Angeles") in Los Angeles, California.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:3-4) She was a kid who liked to draw and create [stop-motion films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop-motion_films "Stop-motion films").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6) She credited [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street") as an early influence sparking her interest in creating animations that combined [live action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_action "Live action"), sound, and pictures.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6)

Fong graduated from [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") with a [Bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in art.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:2-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-8) During college, she made a project that led her to start her career in [WGBH Public Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGBH-TV "WGBH-TV").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6) Her first job at WGBH was as [animator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animator "Animator") for the [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBS "PBS") show "[Where is the World Is Carmen Sandiego?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Where_in_the_World_Is_Carmen_Sandiego%3F_(game_show) "Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego? (game show)")"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:4-10)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Karin_Fong&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1990s Fong moved back to LA and got a job at the West Coast branch of the advertising agency [R/Greenberg Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R/GA "R/GA") (RGA/LA), a studio known for designing opening title sequences for films like [_Seven_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_(1995_film) "Seven (1995 film)"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:5-11)_[Die Hard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die\_Hard "Die Hard")_, _[Alien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien\_(film) "Alien (film)")_, and _[Ghostbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostbusters "Ghostbusters")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6) In 1996, RGA/LA changed its name to Imaginary Forces (stylized as IF) with Fong becoming the founding member of the new studio.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:4-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:5-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-12) Working at Imaginary Forces, Fong met [Joseph McGinty Nichol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McG "McG") as her client.

[Joseph McGinty Nichol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McG "McG") suggested her a job as creative officer at his American production company, [Wonderland Sound and Vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderland_Sound_and_Vision "Wonderland Sound and Vision") in 2001 and started to work more with him.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6)

Fong is a member of the [Alliance Graphique Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Graphique_Internationale "Alliance Graphique Internationale") (AGI).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-13)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Television director

**Karin Fong** is an American [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards")-winning director and designer[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:0-1) based in [Los Angeles, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). She is a co-founder of Imaginary Forces,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-2) a design studio and creative agency best known for its portfolio of work in [main title design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_title_design "Film title design") for [television series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show") and [motion pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_pictures "Motion pictures").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-3) Fong was awarded the 2018 AIGA Medal, the highest distinction in the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") in the U.S., in recognition of her achievements as a [visual storyteller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_narrative "Visual narrative"), [motion graphics designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_graphic_design "Motion graphic design"), and director.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:3-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-5)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Karin_Fong&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Fong was born in 1971 in [Canoga Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoga_Park,_Los_Angeles "Canoga Park, Los Angeles") in Los Angeles, California.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:3-4) She was a kid who liked to draw and create [stop-motion films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop-motion_films "Stop-motion films").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6) She credited [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street") as an early influence sparking her interest in creating animations that combined [live action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_action "Live action"), sound, and pictures.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6)

Fong graduated from [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") with a [Bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in art.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:2-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-8) During college, she made a project that led her to start her career in [WGBH Public Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGBH-TV "WGBH-TV").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6) Her first job at WGBH was as [animator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animator "Animator") for the [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBS "PBS") show "[Where is the World Is Carmen Sandiego?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Where_in_the_World_Is_Carmen_Sandiego%3F_(game_show) "Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego? (game show)")"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:4-10)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Karin_Fong&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1990s Fong moved back to LA and got a job at the West Coast branch of the advertising agency [R/Greenberg Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R/GA "R/GA") (RGA/LA), a studio known for designing opening title sequences for films like [_Seven_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_(1995_film) "Seven (1995 film)"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:5-11)_[Die Hard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die\_Hard "Die Hard")_, _[Alien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien\_(film) "Alien (film)")_, and _[Ghostbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostbusters "Ghostbusters")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6) In 1996, RGA/LA changed its name to Imaginary Forces (stylized as IF) with Fong becoming the founding member of the new studio.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:4-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:5-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-12) Working at Imaginary Forces, Fong met [Joseph McGinty Nichol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McG "McG") as her client.

[Joseph McGinty Nichol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McG "McG") suggested her a job as creative officer at his American production company, [Wonderland Sound and Vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderland_Sound_and_Vision "Wonderland Sound and Vision") in 2001 and started to work more with him.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:1-6)

Fong is a member of the [Alliance Graphique Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Graphique_Internationale "Alliance Graphique Internationale") (AGI).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-13)

## Contributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Karin_Fong&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Contributions")]

Karin Fong has contributed to various title designs for film and television.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Fong#cite_note-:2-7)

*   [The Island of Dr.Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Island_of_Dr._Moreau_(1996_film) "The Island of Dr. Moreau (1996 film)") (1996)
*   [Mimic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimic_(film) "Mimic (film)") (1997)
*   [Dead Man on Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Man_on_Campus "Dead Man on Campus") (1998)
*   [Charlie's Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie's_Angels_(2000_film) "Charlie's Angels (2000 film)") (2000)
*   [Daredevil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daredevil_(film) "Daredevil (film)") (2003)
*   [Hellboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellboy_(2004_film) "Hellboy (2004 film)") (2004)
*   [Charlotte's Web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte's_Web_(2006_film) "Charlotte's Web (2006 film)") (2006)
*   [Terminator: Salvation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminator_Salvation "Terminator Salvation") (2009)
*   [Boardwalk Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boardwalk_Empire "Boardwalk Empire") (2010)
*   [Rubicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubicon_(TV_series) "Rubicon (TV series)") (2010)
*   [Black Sails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sails_(TV_series) "Black Sails (TV series)") (2014)
*   [Counterpart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterpart_(TV_series) "Counterpart (TV series)") (2017)

The main article for this [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Categories "Help:Categories") is **List of AIGA medalists**.

Persons who have received the award of _Medalist._

"The medal of the AIGA, the most distinguished in the field, is awarded to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication")."
