**Ruth Ansel** (born 1938) is an American graphic designer and art director. She became a co-art director of _[Harper's Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's\_Bazaar "Harper's Bazaar")_ in the 1960s alongside [Bea Feitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bea_Feitler "Bea Feitler").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:0-1) In the 1970s she was art director of _[The New York Times Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Magazine "The New York Times Magazine")_ and in the 1980s _[House & Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_&\_Garden\_(magazine) "House & Garden (magazine)")_, _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity\_Fair\_(magazine) "Vanity Fair (magazine)")_, and _[Vogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue\_(magazine) "Vogue (magazine)")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Club-2) She was the first woman to hold these positions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-The_Visionary-3) In 2016, Ansel was awarded the AIGA Medal for her visionary contributions to American graphic design.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_Ansel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Ansel was born in and grew up in [The Bronx, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-6) where according to her, there "wasn’t much to do except dream of getting out."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:3-7) She attended the [High School of Music and Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_School_of_Music_&_Art "High School of Music & Art") in Manhattan.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:3-7)

After graduating with a Fine Arts degree from [Alfred University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_University "Alfred University")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:0-1) in 1957,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-8) she started working under Bob Cato at [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). She married designer [Bob Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Gill_(artist) "Bob Gill (artist)") who introduced her to the "New York Design Mafia" — [George Lois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lois "George Lois"), [Robert Brownjohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn "Robert Brownjohn"), [Saul Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Bass "Saul Bass"), and [Ivan Chermayeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chermayeff "Ivan Chermayeff") — but the couple later split.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4)

In 1961, Ansel started working at _Harper's Bazaar_ in the Art Department, which at the time was under the directorship of [Marvin Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Israel "Marvin Israel"). Under Israel, she developed a critical eye and to create tension on the page.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-The_Visionary-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4) In 1963, Israel was fired after a falling out with editor-in-chief, [Nancy White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_White_(editor) "Nancy White (editor)"), Ruth Ansel and [Bea Feitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bea_Feitler "Bea Feitler") became co-art directors of _Harper's Bazaar_; they were among the youngest art directors in the history of magazines.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-11) It was in collaboration with [Bea Feitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bea_Feitler "Bea Feitler") and [Richard Avedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Avedon "Richard Avedon") that Ruth Ansel produced the now iconic April 1965 cover of [Jean Shrimpton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Shrimpton "Jean Shrimpton") with a winking eye and a bright pink "helmet" that was cut and pasted from day-glo paper.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9) In 1974, she left _Harper's_ to become the first female art director of _[The New York Times Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Magazine "The New York Times Magazine")._ In 1983, she revamped _[House & Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_&\_Garden\_(magazine) "House & Garden (magazine)")_ and in the 1984 joined _Vanity Fair_ as art director.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-The_Visionary-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4) Ansel has collaborated for over four decades with photographers, illustrators and artists such as [Richard Avedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Avedon "Richard Avedon"), [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"), [Peter Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Beard "Peter Beard"), [Bruce Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Weber_(photographer) "Bruce Weber (photographer)") and [Annie Leibovitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Leibovitz "Annie Leibovitz").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-12)

In 1992, Ansel opened her own design studio where she continues to produce groundbreaking content today. In the past she designed the _Dark Odyssey_ by [Phillip Jones Griffiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Jones_Griffiths "Philip Jones Griffiths"), _The Sixties_ by [Richard Avedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Avedon "Richard Avedon"), _Women_ and _The White Oak Dance Project_ by Annie Leibovitz. She has also produced ad campaigns for [Versace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versace "Versace"), [Club Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Monaco "Club Monaco"), and [Karl Lagerfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Lagerfeld "Karl Lagerfeld").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Ruth_Ansel-13) Current projects include a book for photographer [Jerry Schatzberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Schatzberg "Jerry Schatzberg") and a book on the life and work of jewelry designer [Elsa Peretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Peretti "Elsa Peretti").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Ruth_Ansel-13)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_Ansel&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Legacy")]

In 2008, the [Wolfsonian-FIU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfsonian-FIU "Wolfsonian-FIU") organized an exhibition titled, _The Thoughts on Democracy: Reinterpreting Norman Rockwell’s Four Freedoms._ Ansel was one of 55 leading designers invited to contribute a poster based on the "Four Freedoms" posters created in 1943 by American illustrator [Norman Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Rockwell "Norman Rockwell").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-14) In 2009 she was invited to present her work at [Moderna Museet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderna_Museet "Moderna Museet") in Stockholm, Sweden.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Club-2) In 2010, as the first book of the [Hall of Femmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_of_Femmes "Hall of Femmes") series, _Hall of Femmes: Ruth Ansel_ was published.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:02-15) A book designed by Hjarta Smarta, highlighting her forty-year career and taking a look at what it was like to be the first woman in these positions.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9) In 2011, Ansel was the recipient of the [Art Director's Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club_of_New_York "Art Directors Club of New York") prestigious [Hall of Fame Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club_Hall_of_Fame "Art Directors Club Hall of Fame").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Club-2)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:02-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-sva2011-17)

**Ruth Ansel** (born 1938) is an American graphic designer and art director. She became a co-art director of _[Harper's Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's\_Bazaar "Harper's Bazaar")_ in the 1960s alongside [Bea Feitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bea_Feitler "Bea Feitler").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:0-1) In the 1970s she was art director of _[The New York Times Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Magazine "The New York Times Magazine")_ and in the 1980s _[House & Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_&\_Garden\_(magazine) "House & Garden (magazine)")_, _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity\_Fair\_(magazine) "Vanity Fair (magazine)")_, and _[Vogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue\_(magazine) "Vogue (magazine)")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Club-2) She was the first woman to hold these positions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-The_Visionary-3) In 2016, Ansel was awarded the AIGA Medal for her visionary contributions to American graphic design.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_Ansel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Ansel was born in and grew up in [The Bronx, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-6) where according to her, there "wasn’t much to do except dream of getting out."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:3-7) She attended the [High School of Music and Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_School_of_Music_&_Art "High School of Music & Art") in Manhattan.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:3-7)

After graduating with a Fine Arts degree from [Alfred University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_University "Alfred University")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:0-1) in 1957,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-8) she started working under Bob Cato at [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). She married designer [Bob Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Gill_(artist) "Bob Gill (artist)") who introduced her to the "New York Design Mafia" — [George Lois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lois "George Lois"), [Robert Brownjohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn "Robert Brownjohn"), [Saul Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Bass "Saul Bass"), and [Ivan Chermayeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chermayeff "Ivan Chermayeff") — but the couple later split.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4)

In 1961, Ansel started working at _Harper's Bazaar_ in the Art Department, which at the time was under the directorship of [Marvin Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Israel "Marvin Israel"). Under Israel, she developed a critical eye and to create tension on the page.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-The_Visionary-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4) In 1963, Israel was fired after a falling out with editor-in-chief, [Nancy White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_White_(editor) "Nancy White (editor)"), Ruth Ansel and [Bea Feitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bea_Feitler "Bea Feitler") became co-art directors of _Harper's Bazaar_; they were among the youngest art directors in the history of magazines.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-11) It was in collaboration with [Bea Feitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bea_Feitler "Bea Feitler") and [Richard Avedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Avedon "Richard Avedon") that Ruth Ansel produced the now iconic April 1965 cover of [Jean Shrimpton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Shrimpton "Jean Shrimpton") with a winking eye and a bright pink "helmet" that was cut and pasted from day-glo paper.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9) In 1974, she left _Harper's_ to become the first female art director of _[The New York Times Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Magazine "The New York Times Magazine")._ In 1983, she revamped _[House & Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_&\_Garden\_(magazine) "House & Garden (magazine)")_ and in the 1984 joined _Vanity Fair_ as art director.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-The_Visionary-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:2-4) Ansel has collaborated for over four decades with photographers, illustrators and artists such as [Richard Avedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Avedon "Richard Avedon"), [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"), [Peter Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Beard "Peter Beard"), [Bruce Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Weber_(photographer) "Bruce Weber (photographer)") and [Annie Leibovitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Leibovitz "Annie Leibovitz").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-12)

In 1992, Ansel opened her own design studio where she continues to produce groundbreaking content today. In the past she designed the _Dark Odyssey_ by [Phillip Jones Griffiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Jones_Griffiths "Philip Jones Griffiths"), _The Sixties_ by [Richard Avedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Avedon "Richard Avedon"), _Women_ and _The White Oak Dance Project_ by Annie Leibovitz. She has also produced ad campaigns for [Versace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versace "Versace"), [Club Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Monaco "Club Monaco"), and [Karl Lagerfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Lagerfeld "Karl Lagerfeld").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Ruth_Ansel-13) Current projects include a book for photographer [Jerry Schatzberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Schatzberg "Jerry Schatzberg") and a book on the life and work of jewelry designer [Elsa Peretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Peretti "Elsa Peretti").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Ruth_Ansel-13)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_Ansel&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Legacy")]

In 2008, the [Wolfsonian-FIU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfsonian-FIU "Wolfsonian-FIU") organized an exhibition titled, _The Thoughts on Democracy: Reinterpreting Norman Rockwell’s Four Freedoms._ Ansel was one of 55 leading designers invited to contribute a poster based on the "Four Freedoms" posters created in 1943 by American illustrator [Norman Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Rockwell "Norman Rockwell").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-14) In 2009 she was invited to present her work at [Moderna Museet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderna_Museet "Moderna Museet") in Stockholm, Sweden.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Club-2) In 2010, as the first book of the [Hall of Femmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_of_Femmes "Hall of Femmes") series, _Hall of Femmes: Ruth Ansel_ was published.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:02-15) A book designed by Hjarta Smarta, highlighting her forty-year career and taking a look at what it was like to be the first woman in these positions.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:1-9) In 2011, Ansel was the recipient of the [Art Director's Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club_of_New_York "Art Directors Club of New York") prestigious [Hall of Fame Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club_Hall_of_Fame "Art Directors Club Hall of Fame").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-Club-2)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-:02-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ansel#cite_note-sva2011-17)

**J. Abbott Miller** or **Abbott Miller** (born 1962)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-aiga-1) is an American graphic designer and writer, and a partner at [Pentagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagram_(design_studio) "Pentagram (design studio)"), which he joined in 1999.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=J._Abbott_Miller&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Abbott Miller was born in [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") and studied at the [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union") School of Art in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-ae-pro-3)

In 1989 he founded the multidisciplinary studio Design/Writing/Research where, in collaboration with [Ellen Lupton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Lupton "Ellen Lupton"), he pioneered the concept of “designer as author” undertaking projects in which content and form are developed in a symbiotic relationship. He joined the New York office of the design firm [Pentagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagram_(design_firm) "Pentagram (design firm)") as a partner in 1999. Miller is married to Ellen Lupton. Miller's projects are often concerned with the cultural role of design and the public life of the written word. At Pentagram he leads a team designing identities, exhibitions, environmental graphics, books, magazines, and web and interactive projects. He is the designer and editor of _[2wice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2wice "2wice")_ magazine.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-aiga-1)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=J._Abbott_Miller&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Awards")]

Miller has received numerous design honors, including medals from the [Society for Publication Designers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_for_Publication_Designers?action=edit&redlink=1 "Society for Publication Designers (page does not exist)"), the [Art Directors Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club "Art Directors Club"), and the [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA "AIGA"). In 1994, Miller––together with [Ellen Lupton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Lupton "Ellen Lupton")––was awarded the first annual [Chrysler Award for Innovation in Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Award_for_Innovation_in_Design "Chrysler Award for Innovation in Design"). He is also the recipient of the [Augustus St. Gaudens Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_St._Gaudens_Award?action=edit&redlink=1 "Augustus St. Gaudens Award (page does not exist)") from [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union"), and received the [AIGA medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_medal "AIGA medal") in 2014.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-aiga-1) He is a visiting critic in the Graduate Design Program at the [Maryland Institute College of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland_Institute_College_of_Art "Maryland Institute College of Art") in Baltimore. His work is represented in the collections of the [Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper-Hewitt_National_Design_Museum "Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum"), the [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art"), the [Art Institute of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Institute_of_Chicago "Art Institute of Chicago"), and the [Bibliothèque nationale de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioth%C3%A8que_nationale_de_France "Bibliothèque nationale de France"). His work and critical writing has appeared in Eye, Print, I.D., and other publications, and he is the co-author of four books, including _Design/Writing/Research: Writing on Graphic Design_. A survey of his design work was published by [Princeton Architectural Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_Architectural_Press "Princeton Architectural Press") in September 2014.

**J. Abbott Miller** or **Abbott Miller** (born 1962)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-aiga-1) is an American graphic designer and writer, and a partner at [Pentagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagram_(design_studio) "Pentagram (design studio)"), which he joined in 1999.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=J._Abbott_Miller&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Abbott Miller was born in [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") and studied at the [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union") School of Art in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-ae-pro-3)

In 1989 he founded the multidisciplinary studio Design/Writing/Research where, in collaboration with [Ellen Lupton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Lupton "Ellen Lupton"), he pioneered the concept of “designer as author” undertaking projects in which content and form are developed in a symbiotic relationship. He joined the New York office of the design firm [Pentagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagram_(design_firm) "Pentagram (design firm)") as a partner in 1999. Miller is married to Ellen Lupton. Miller's projects are often concerned with the cultural role of design and the public life of the written word. At Pentagram he leads a team designing identities, exhibitions, environmental graphics, books, magazines, and web and interactive projects. He is the designer and editor of _[2wice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2wice "2wice")_ magazine.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-aiga-1)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=J._Abbott_Miller&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Awards")]

Miller has received numerous design honors, including medals from the [Society for Publication Designers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_for_Publication_Designers?action=edit&redlink=1 "Society for Publication Designers (page does not exist)"), the [Art Directors Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club "Art Directors Club"), and the [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA "AIGA"). In 1994, Miller––together with [Ellen Lupton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Lupton "Ellen Lupton")––was awarded the first annual [Chrysler Award for Innovation in Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Award_for_Innovation_in_Design "Chrysler Award for Innovation in Design"). He is also the recipient of the [Augustus St. Gaudens Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_St._Gaudens_Award?action=edit&redlink=1 "Augustus St. Gaudens Award (page does not exist)") from [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union"), and received the [AIGA medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_medal "AIGA medal") in 2014.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Abbott_Miller#cite_note-aiga-1) He is a visiting critic in the Graduate Design Program at the [Maryland Institute College of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland_Institute_College_of_Art "Maryland Institute College of Art") in Baltimore. His work is represented in the collections of the [Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper-Hewitt_National_Design_Museum "Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum"), the [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art"), the [Art Institute of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Institute_of_Chicago "Art Institute of Chicago"), and the [Bibliothèque nationale de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioth%C3%A8que_nationale_de_France "Bibliothèque nationale de France"). His work and critical writing has appeared in Eye, Print, I.D., and other publications, and he is the co-author of four books, including _Design/Writing/Research: Writing on Graphic Design_. A survey of his design work was published by [Princeton Architectural Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_Architectural_Press "Princeton Architectural Press") in September 2014.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American graphic designer

**Alexander Isley** (born (1961-11-16)November 16, 1961)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-who-1) is an American [graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_designer "Graphic designer") and educator.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Isley&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Alexander Isley was born in [Durham, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_North_Carolina "Durham, North Carolina") and studied at [Durham Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Academy,_North_Carolina "Durham Academy, North Carolina"), the [University of North Carolina School of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_School_of_the_Arts "University of North Carolina School of the Arts") (high school visual arts diploma).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Isley initially wanted to become an architect like his father but discovered design upon enrolling in [North Carolina State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_University "North Carolina State University"), where he received a degree in Environmental Design.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-3) He later attended the [Cooper Union School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union_School_of_Art "Cooper Union School of Art") in New York and received a BFA in graphic design.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1994, Isley married Veronica Burke.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-4)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Isley&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1984, Isley joined [Tibor Kalman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman "Tibor Kalman")'s influential [M & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M_&_Co._(design_firm) "M & Co. (design firm)") as senior designer. He held this position until 1987, when he joined [_Spy_ Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_(magazine) "Spy (magazine)") in 1987 as the first full-time art director. At _Spy_, he was tasked with building upon Steven Doyle's initial formatting and was awarded gold and silver medals from the Society of Publication Designers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-5) In 1988, he founded Alexander Isley Inc. in New York City.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-6) In 1995, Isley moved the studio to [Redding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redding,_Connecticut "Redding, Connecticut"), [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut "Connecticut").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2) The studio has worked on branding projects for Youth Service America, Armani Jeans and Goodwill, among others.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-7)

In 2004, Isley became the president of [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") New York and an AIGA Fellow in 2013 after being a board member from 1988 to 1990.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:1-9)

In addition to his professional career, Isley taught Design and Typography at the [School of Visual Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Visual_Arts "School of Visual Arts") from 1988 to 1990; Exhibit Design at the [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union") in 1992; and was a Critic and Lecturer at [Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") from 1996 to 2011.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-10)

## Honors and awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Isley&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Honors and awards")]

*   Terry Sanford Scholarship to the University of North Carolina School of the Arts, 1979[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-11)
*   [Art Directors Club of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Directors_Club_of_New_York "Art Directors Club of New York") Herb Lubalin Memorial Award, 1984

## Archives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Isley&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Archives")]

The Alexander Isley Papers [[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-16) at the Special Collections Research Center, [North Carolina State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_University "North Carolina State University") Libraries, Raleigh, covers Isley’s full career and includes initial concept explorations, original artwork, completed materials, and correspondence. An extensive selection of Isley’s poster designs are in the collection of the [Museum of Design, Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Design,_Z%C3%BCrich "Museum of Design, Zürich").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American graphic designer

**Alexander Isley** (born (1961-11-16)November 16, 1961)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-who-1) is an American [graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_designer "Graphic designer") and educator.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Isley&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Alexander Isley was born in [Durham, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_North_Carolina "Durham, North Carolina") and studied at [Durham Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Academy,_North_Carolina "Durham Academy, North Carolina"), the [University of North Carolina School of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_School_of_the_Arts "University of North Carolina School of the Arts") (high school visual arts diploma).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Isley initially wanted to become an architect like his father but discovered design upon enrolling in [North Carolina State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_University "North Carolina State University"), where he received a degree in Environmental Design.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-3) He later attended the [Cooper Union School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union_School_of_Art "Cooper Union School of Art") in New York and received a BFA in graphic design.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1994, Isley married Veronica Burke.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-4)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Isley&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1984, Isley joined [Tibor Kalman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman "Tibor Kalman")'s influential [M & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M_&_Co._(design_firm) "M & Co. (design firm)") as senior designer. He held this position until 1987, when he joined [_Spy_ Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_(magazine) "Spy (magazine)") in 1987 as the first full-time art director. At _Spy_, he was tasked with building upon Steven Doyle's initial formatting and was awarded gold and silver medals from the Society of Publication Designers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-5) In 1988, he founded Alexander Isley Inc. in New York City.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-6) In 1995, Isley moved the studio to [Redding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redding,_Connecticut "Redding, Connecticut"), [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut "Connecticut").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2) The studio has worked on branding projects for Youth Service America, Armani Jeans and Goodwill, among others.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-7)

In 2004, Isley became the president of [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") New York and an AIGA Fellow in 2013 after being a board member from 1988 to 1990.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:0-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-:1-9)

In addition to his professional career, Isley taught Design and Typography at the [School of Visual Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Visual_Arts "School of Visual Arts") from 1988 to 1990; Exhibit Design at the [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union") in 1992; and was a Critic and Lecturer at [Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") from 1996 to 2011.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Isley#cite_note-10)

**Corita Kent** (November 20, 1918 – September 18, 1986), born **Frances Elizabeth Kent** and also known as **Sister Mary Corita Kent**, was an American artist, designer and educator, and former [religious sister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_sister "Religious sister"). Key themes in her work included [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") and [social justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_justice "Social justice"). She was also a teacher at the [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1)

Corita was born Frances Elizabeth Kent on November 20 1918. At 18, Kent entered the [Sisters of the Immaculate Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisters_of_the_Immaculate_Heart_of_Mary "Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary"), which were known to be very progressive and welcomed creativity. Frances joined a teaching order, taking the name Sister Mary Corita. She received a bachelor's degree at [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College") and a master's degree at [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California"). She was the head of the art department at Immaculate Heart College[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) where she also taught a wide variety of different painting styles. Her artwork contained her own spiritual expression and love for God.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Art_Story-2)

Kent's primary medium was screen printing, also known as [serigraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serigraphy "Serigraphy").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-3) She became self-taught after she sent away for a DIY silk screening kit.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-4) Her innovative methods pushed back the limitations of two-dimensional media of the times. Kent's emphasis on printing was partially due to her wish for democratic outreach, as she wished for affordable art for the masses.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5) Her artwork, with its messages of love and peace, was particularly popular during the [social upheavals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") of the 1960s and 1970s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-6)

Due to opposition from Cardinal [James McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Francis_McIntyre "James Francis McIntyre") (who had a particular dislike for Kent), the sisters would eventually be forced out of their schools in Los Angeles—with the exception of the college—and most of the sisters left the order entirely, while keeping the larger school. Kent, however, would move to the East Coast and begin to work independently.

After a cancer diagnosis in the early 1970s, she entered an extremely prolific period in her career, including the [Rainbow Swash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Swash "Rainbow Swash") design on the LNG storage tank in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), and the 1985 version of the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service")'s special _[Love](https://web.archive.org/web/20160724032655/http://cbsnews3.cbsistatic.com/hub/i/r/2016/04/02/4c560ba5-fdf3-4096-9ba6-b33ba1fb8dd5/resize/620x465/8cea1ccbd93ede8fa0ad6df34dff1ff5/corita-kent-love-stamp-usps.jpg)_ stamp.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-7)

In recent years, Corita has gained increased recognition for her role in the [pop art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_art "Pop art") movement. Critics and theorists previously failed to count her work as part of any mainstream "canon," but in the last few years there has been a resurgence of attention given to Kent. As both a nun and a woman making art in the twentieth century, she was in many ways cast to the margins of the different movements she was a part of.

Corita's art was her activism, and her spiritually-informed social commentary promoted love and tolerance.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Frances Elizabeth Kent, fifth child of Robert Vincent and Edith Genevieve, was born in Fort Dodge, Iowa on November 20, 1918. Kent's parents were artistically inclined, especially her father, and always encouraged her art. In junior high, Corita and her siblings attended Blessed Sacrament School which was partially staffed by [Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisters_of_the_Immaculate_Heart_of_Mary "Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary"). When attending junior high, Kent's art potential was noticed by several nuns.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pacatte-2017-8) Kent graduated from Los Angeles Catholic Girls' High School in 1936.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pacatte-2017-8)

Upon entering the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") order of IHM sisters in Los Angeles in 1936, Kent took the name Sister Mary Corita. She took classes at Otis (now [Otis College of Art and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis_College_of_Art_and_Design "Otis College of Art and Design")) and [Chouinard Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouinard_Art_Institute "Chouinard Art Institute"), and received a BA degree from [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College") in 1941. She received a MA degree at the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California") (USC) in [Art History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_history "Art history") in 1951. Kent recalled in an oral history interview with [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") that she learned serigraphy during this time from Maria Sodi de Ramos Martínez, the widow of Mexican muralist [Alfredo Ramos Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfredo_Ramos_Mart%C3%ADnez "Alfredo Ramos Martínez").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-9)

### Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

Between 1938 and 1968 Kent lived and worked in the Immaculate Heart Community.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Eye_2000-10) She taught in the [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College") and became the chair of its art department in 1964.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Her classes at Immaculate Heart were an avant-garde mecca for prominent, ground-breaking artists and inventors, such as [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock"), [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"), [Saul Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Bass "Saul Bass"), [Buckminster Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckminster_Fuller "Buckminster Fuller") and [Charles & Ray Eames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_and_Ray_Eames "Charles and Ray Eames").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-11) Kent credited [Charles Eames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Eames "Charles Eames"), [Buckminster Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckminster_Fuller "Buckminster Fuller"), and art historian Dr. [Alois Schardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alois_Schardt?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alois Schardt (page does not exist)") for their important roles in her intellectual and artistic growth.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-12) By the early 1950s, she had a unique and well-known aesthetic and teaching style that clergy members from all over the country were sent to be educated at Immaculate Heart College. Her students were drawn to her selflessness and teaching methods such as large class assignments like asking students to create 200 drawings or take three hours to draw their arm without looking at what they were creating.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-The_Getty_Iris-2015-13)

Kent toured widely the following decade. After the [Second Vatican Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Vatican_Council "Second Vatican Council"), Kent transformed Immaculate Heart College's annual Mary's Day procession into a community celebration which was part of the sister's campaign to bring secular people together. During this time, Kent's work became increasingly political, addressing events such as the Vietnam War and humanitarian crises. For example, she was commissioned by the Physicians for Social Responsibility to create what she called "we can create life without war" billboards.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Tensions between the order and church leadership were mounting, with the Los Angeles archdiocese criticizing the college as "liberal" and [Cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_(Catholic_Church) "Cardinal (Catholic Church)")[James McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Francis_McIntyre "James Francis McIntyre") labeling the college as "communist" and Kent's work as "blasphemous."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-National_Catholic_Reporter-2016-14) Due to this, Kent returned to secular life in 1968 as Corita Kent. Most sisters followed suit and the Immaculate Heart College closed in 1980.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-15) Corita Kent also embraced the many different revolutionary movements going on in the world at this time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-16) These movements included the anti-Vietnam War movement, Civil Rights, and Women's Rights.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-17)

Kent created several hundred serigraph designs, for posters, [book covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_cover "Book cover"), and [murals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural "Mural"). Her work includes the 1985 [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") stamp _[Love](https://web.archive.org/web/20160724032655/http://cbsnews3.cbsistatic.com/hub/i/r/2016/04/02/4c560ba5-fdf3-4096-9ba6-b33ba1fb8dd5/resize/620x465/8cea1ccbd93ede8fa0ad6df34dff1ff5/corita-kent-love-stamp-usps.jpg)_[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-18) and the 1971 _[Rainbow Swash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow\_Swash "Rainbow Swash")_, the largest copyrighted work of art in the world, covering a 150-foot (46 m) high natural gas tank in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-19) She did not attend the unveiling of the _Love_ stamp because she wanted it to happen at the United Nations and was not happy with the message that was sent when the design was unveiled on the Love Boat.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Her 1985 work "love is hard work" was made in response. The stamp itself sold successfully—over 700 million times.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-National_Catholic_Reporter-2016-14) Kent was also commissioned to create work for the 1964 World's Fair in New York, and the 1965 IBM Christmas display in New York.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Her 1951 print, _[The Lord is with Thee](https://web.archive.org/web/20161221034421/http://collections.lacma.org/node/233635)_ had won first prizes in printmaking at the Los Angeles County Museum of History, Science, Art, and at the California State Fair.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5)

Kent's work has been exhibited extensively beginning in 1952. By the 1960s, Kent had already shown work at 230 exhibitions across the country and her work was included in the collections the Achenbach Foundation Graphic Arts, the [Fogg museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fogg_museum "Fogg museum"), the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Art "Los Angeles County Museum of Art"), the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"), the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art"), the [National Gallery of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Art "National Gallery of Art"), the [National Serigraph Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Serigraph_Society "National Serigraph Society"), the [Norman Rockwell Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Rockwell_Museum "Norman Rockwell Museum"), the [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art"), the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution"), and the [Whitney Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Museum_of_American_Art "Whitney Museum of American Art").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-The_Getty_Iris-2015-13)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Exhibitions_Corita_Art_Center-20)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Death")]

Corita Kent was diagnosed with ovarian cancer in 1974. After this diagnosis, in the Back Bay of Boston, Kent confined her art to water color painting and only pursued printmaking in order to say something substantive.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Kennelly-2004-21) The _Papers of Corita_ revealed Kent had kept two calendars towards the end of her life. This displayed that Kent, in the midst of fighting cancer, followed a strict diet, answered and wrote letters, and wanted to live and continue to create art.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pacatte-2017-8)

She died on September 18, 1986, in Watertown Massachusetts at the age of sixty-seven.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Kennelly-2004-21) She left her copyrights and unsold works to the Immaculate Heart Community formed by the former IHM sisters in Los Angeles.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography2-22)

## Artistic style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Artistic style")]

Corita Kent worked at the intersection of several powerful—and at times contradictory—cultural, political, and religious influences. Corita Kent, inspired by the works of [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"), began using [popular culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_culture "Popular culture") as raw material for her work in 1962.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5) Her screen prints often incorporated archetypical product brands of American [consumerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumerism "Consumerism") alongside spiritual texts. Her design process involved appropriating an original advertising graphic to suit her idea; for example, she would tear, rip, or crumple the image, then re-photograph it. She often used grocery store signage, texts from scripture, newspaper clippings, song lyrics, and writings from literary greats such as [Gertrude Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrude_Stein "Gertrude Stein"), [E. E. Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._E._Cummings "E. E. Cummings"), and [Albert Camus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Camus "Albert Camus") as the textual focal point of her work.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-23)

E. E. Cummings was one of Kent's earliest and strongest influences. She quotes him in her work separately more than a dozen times and was inspired by a line from one of his lectures to create an entire series of alphabet prints.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-The_Getty_Iris-2015-13) In her 1966 piece _Tame It's Not_, she uses quotes from Winnie the Pooh, Kierkegaard, and an ad slogan for men's cologne. Using everyday consumer items, like Wonderbread, she was able to bring words and thoughts about her religion to a familiar product that people saw and used every day.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Art_Story-2) By creating juxtaposition between formally acknowledged or respected "art" and the art Corita saw in her everyday world—at the supermarket, on a walk, in the classroom—she elevated the banal to the holy. "Like a priest, a shaman, a magician, she could pass her hands over the commonest of the everyday, the superficial, the oh-so-ordinary, and make it a vehicle of the luminous, the only, and the hope filled," noted Corita's friend, theologian [Harvey Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Cox "Harvey Cox").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-24)

Corita's earliest work was mostly iconographic, drawing inspiration and material from the Bible and other religious sources. Her style is heavily text-based, with scripture passages or positive quotes often encompassing entire compositions with bold and highly saturated typefaces. Despite the often surreal or disorienting compositions of her works, her pieces are "always _about_ something."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5) By the 1960s, her work started becoming increasingly political.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1)

Kent produced her oeuvre during her time at Immaculate Heart College in Los Angeles in response to the Catholic reform in the 1960s by the Vatican Council II as well as several political and social issues happening at the time.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Newhouse-2000-25) Her work itself aided in the Vatican II movement, a movement to modernize and make relevant the Catholic Church. Kent's use of English church texts in her work, for example, made an impact on the Vatican II's efforts to normalize conducting Mass in English.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-26) Because of her strongly political art, she and others left their order to create the Immaculate Heart Community in 1970 to avoid problems with their archdiocese.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Newhouse-2000-25)

The "_Big G_" logo that Kent appropriated from General Mills was to stress the idea of 'goodness', while the elements from Esso gasoline ads were meant to project the internal power within humans.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pagel-2000-27) Unsurprisingly, a Christian subtext does underscore several of her artworks, but not all, which are open to interpretation.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pagel-2000-27)

One of Kent's prints, _love your brother_ (1969), depicts photographs of Martin Luther King Jr. overlaid with her handwritten words, "The king is dead. Love your brother," producing one of her more serious artworks, and presenting her views on politics and human nature.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-28) Her collages took popular images, often with twisted or reversed words, to comment on the political unrest of the period, many of which could have been found at any number of marches or demonstrations, some of which she attended herself.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pagel-2000-27)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

Kent had solo exhibitions at the [National Museum of Women in the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Women_in_the_Arts "National Museum of Women in the Arts") (_R(ad)ical Love: Sister Mary Corita_,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-National_Museum_of_Women_in_the_Arts-29) 2012) and her work is in several art museums, including the [Whitney Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Museum_of_American_Art "Whitney Museum of American Art"), the [Museum of Fine Arts, Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Fine_Arts,_Boston "Museum of Fine Arts, Boston") and [The Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"). An archive is dedicated to her at the [Immaculate Heart Community Headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Immaculate Heart High School (Los Angeles)") in Hollywood, CA. Some of Sister Corita's papers and early artwork are in Schlesinger Library, in the Radcliffe Institute, Harvard University.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-30) Recent solo exhibitions of Kent's work include _Someday is Now: The Art of Corita Kent_[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-31) at the Tang Museum at [Skidmore College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore_College "Skidmore College") and _There Will Be New Rules Next Week_ at [Dundee Contemporary Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee_Contemporary_Arts "Dundee Contemporary Arts").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-32)

The Corita Art Center (CAC), a gallery and archive dedicated to preserving and promoting the work and spirit of Corita Kent, was originally founded as the Corita Prints in 1969 in North Hollywood. It changed its name when it moved to the Immaculate Heart property in 1997 and is located within the offices of the Immaculate Heart Community Headquarters in Hollywood, CA.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-33) In September, 2024, the CAC announced that it would move to a new location in the [Arts District of Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_District,_Los_Angeles "Arts District, Los Angeles") in 2025.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-34) The Corita Art Center opened in the Los Angeles Arts District on March 8, 2025.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-35)

Corita Kent received the American Institute of Graphic Arts Medal in 2016.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dackerman-36)

Kent was one of the nuns featured in _[Rebel Hearts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel\_Hearts\_(film) "Rebel Hearts (film)")_, a 2021 American documentary directed, produced, and edited by [Pedro Kos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Kos "Pedro Kos"). It had its world premiere at the [2021 Sundance Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Sundance_Film_Festival "2021 Sundance Film Festival") on January 29, 2021.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-37) It received a [limited release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_release "Limited release") on June 25, 2021, before digital streaming on [Discovery+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery+ "Discovery+") starting June 27, 2021.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-38)

In 2023 the Catticus Corporation was granted $700,000[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-39) by the [National Endowment for the Humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Humanities "National Endowment for the Humanities") to produce a documentary, titled "You Should Never Blink", about the rebellious life of the “pop art nun” Corita Kent.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-40)
