**Corita Kent** (November 20, 1918 – September 18, 1986), born **Frances Elizabeth Kent** and also known as **Sister Mary Corita Kent**, was an American artist, designer and educator, and former [religious sister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_sister "Religious sister"). Key themes in her work included [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") and [social justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_justice "Social justice"). She was also a teacher at the [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1)

Corita was born Frances Elizabeth Kent on November 20 1918. At 18, Kent entered the [Sisters of the Immaculate Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisters_of_the_Immaculate_Heart_of_Mary "Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary"), which were known to be very progressive and welcomed creativity. Frances joined a teaching order, taking the name Sister Mary Corita. She received a bachelor's degree at [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College") and a master's degree at [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California"). She was the head of the art department at Immaculate Heart College[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) where she also taught a wide variety of different painting styles. Her artwork contained her own spiritual expression and love for God.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Art_Story-2)

Kent's primary medium was screen printing, also known as [serigraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serigraphy "Serigraphy").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-3) She became self-taught after she sent away for a DIY silk screening kit.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-4) Her innovative methods pushed back the limitations of two-dimensional media of the times. Kent's emphasis on printing was partially due to her wish for democratic outreach, as she wished for affordable art for the masses.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5) Her artwork, with its messages of love and peace, was particularly popular during the [social upheavals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") of the 1960s and 1970s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-6)

Due to opposition from Cardinal [James McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Francis_McIntyre "James Francis McIntyre") (who had a particular dislike for Kent), the sisters would eventually be forced out of their schools in Los Angeles—with the exception of the college—and most of the sisters left the order entirely, while keeping the larger school. Kent, however, would move to the East Coast and begin to work independently.

After a cancer diagnosis in the early 1970s, she entered an extremely prolific period in her career, including the [Rainbow Swash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Swash "Rainbow Swash") design on the LNG storage tank in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), and the 1985 version of the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service")'s special _[Love](https://web.archive.org/web/20160724032655/http://cbsnews3.cbsistatic.com/hub/i/r/2016/04/02/4c560ba5-fdf3-4096-9ba6-b33ba1fb8dd5/resize/620x465/8cea1ccbd93ede8fa0ad6df34dff1ff5/corita-kent-love-stamp-usps.jpg)_ stamp.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-7)

In recent years, Corita has gained increased recognition for her role in the [pop art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_art "Pop art") movement. Critics and theorists previously failed to count her work as part of any mainstream "canon," but in the last few years there has been a resurgence of attention given to Kent. As both a nun and a woman making art in the twentieth century, she was in many ways cast to the margins of the different movements she was a part of.

Corita's art was her activism, and her spiritually-informed social commentary promoted love and tolerance.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Frances Elizabeth Kent, fifth child of Robert Vincent and Edith Genevieve, was born in Fort Dodge, Iowa on November 20, 1918. Kent's parents were artistically inclined, especially her father, and always encouraged her art. In junior high, Corita and her siblings attended Blessed Sacrament School which was partially staffed by [Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisters_of_the_Immaculate_Heart_of_Mary "Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary"). When attending junior high, Kent's art potential was noticed by several nuns.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pacatte-2017-8) Kent graduated from Los Angeles Catholic Girls' High School in 1936.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pacatte-2017-8)

Upon entering the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") order of IHM sisters in Los Angeles in 1936, Kent took the name Sister Mary Corita. She took classes at Otis (now [Otis College of Art and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis_College_of_Art_and_Design "Otis College of Art and Design")) and [Chouinard Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouinard_Art_Institute "Chouinard Art Institute"), and received a BA degree from [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College") in 1941. She received a MA degree at the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California") (USC) in [Art History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_history "Art history") in 1951. Kent recalled in an oral history interview with [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") that she learned serigraphy during this time from Maria Sodi de Ramos Martínez, the widow of Mexican muralist [Alfredo Ramos Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfredo_Ramos_Mart%C3%ADnez "Alfredo Ramos Martínez").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-9)

### Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

Between 1938 and 1968 Kent lived and worked in the Immaculate Heart Community.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Eye_2000-10) She taught in the [Immaculate Heart College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_College "Immaculate Heart College") and became the chair of its art department in 1964.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Her classes at Immaculate Heart were an avant-garde mecca for prominent, ground-breaking artists and inventors, such as [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock"), [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"), [Saul Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Bass "Saul Bass"), [Buckminster Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckminster_Fuller "Buckminster Fuller") and [Charles & Ray Eames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_and_Ray_Eames "Charles and Ray Eames").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-11) Kent credited [Charles Eames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Eames "Charles Eames"), [Buckminster Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckminster_Fuller "Buckminster Fuller"), and art historian Dr. [Alois Schardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alois_Schardt?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alois Schardt (page does not exist)") for their important roles in her intellectual and artistic growth.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-12) By the early 1950s, she had a unique and well-known aesthetic and teaching style that clergy members from all over the country were sent to be educated at Immaculate Heart College. Her students were drawn to her selflessness and teaching methods such as large class assignments like asking students to create 200 drawings or take three hours to draw their arm without looking at what they were creating.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-The_Getty_Iris-2015-13)

Kent toured widely the following decade. After the [Second Vatican Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Vatican_Council "Second Vatican Council"), Kent transformed Immaculate Heart College's annual Mary's Day procession into a community celebration which was part of the sister's campaign to bring secular people together. During this time, Kent's work became increasingly political, addressing events such as the Vietnam War and humanitarian crises. For example, she was commissioned by the Physicians for Social Responsibility to create what she called "we can create life without war" billboards.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Tensions between the order and church leadership were mounting, with the Los Angeles archdiocese criticizing the college as "liberal" and [Cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_(Catholic_Church) "Cardinal (Catholic Church)")[James McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Francis_McIntyre "James Francis McIntyre") labeling the college as "communist" and Kent's work as "blasphemous."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-National_Catholic_Reporter-2016-14) Due to this, Kent returned to secular life in 1968 as Corita Kent. Most sisters followed suit and the Immaculate Heart College closed in 1980.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-15) Corita Kent also embraced the many different revolutionary movements going on in the world at this time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-16) These movements included the anti-Vietnam War movement, Civil Rights, and Women's Rights.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-17)

Kent created several hundred serigraph designs, for posters, [book covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_cover "Book cover"), and [murals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural "Mural"). Her work includes the 1985 [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") stamp _[Love](https://web.archive.org/web/20160724032655/http://cbsnews3.cbsistatic.com/hub/i/r/2016/04/02/4c560ba5-fdf3-4096-9ba6-b33ba1fb8dd5/resize/620x465/8cea1ccbd93ede8fa0ad6df34dff1ff5/corita-kent-love-stamp-usps.jpg)_[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-18) and the 1971 _[Rainbow Swash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow\_Swash "Rainbow Swash")_, the largest copyrighted work of art in the world, covering a 150-foot (46 m) high natural gas tank in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-19) She did not attend the unveiling of the _Love_ stamp because she wanted it to happen at the United Nations and was not happy with the message that was sent when the design was unveiled on the Love Boat.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Her 1985 work "love is hard work" was made in response. The stamp itself sold successfully—over 700 million times.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-National_Catholic_Reporter-2016-14) Kent was also commissioned to create work for the 1964 World's Fair in New York, and the 1965 IBM Christmas display in New York.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1) Her 1951 print, _[The Lord is with Thee](https://web.archive.org/web/20161221034421/http://collections.lacma.org/node/233635)_ had won first prizes in printmaking at the Los Angeles County Museum of History, Science, Art, and at the California State Fair.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5)

Kent's work has been exhibited extensively beginning in 1952. By the 1960s, Kent had already shown work at 230 exhibitions across the country and her work was included in the collections the Achenbach Foundation Graphic Arts, the [Fogg museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fogg_museum "Fogg museum"), the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Art "Los Angeles County Museum of Art"), the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"), the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art"), the [National Gallery of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Art "National Gallery of Art"), the [National Serigraph Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Serigraph_Society "National Serigraph Society"), the [Norman Rockwell Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Rockwell_Museum "Norman Rockwell Museum"), the [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art"), the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution"), and the [Whitney Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Museum_of_American_Art "Whitney Museum of American Art").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-The_Getty_Iris-2015-13)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Exhibitions_Corita_Art_Center-20)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Death")]

Corita Kent was diagnosed with ovarian cancer in 1974. After this diagnosis, in the Back Bay of Boston, Kent confined her art to water color painting and only pursued printmaking in order to say something substantive.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Kennelly-2004-21) The _Papers of Corita_ revealed Kent had kept two calendars towards the end of her life. This displayed that Kent, in the midst of fighting cancer, followed a strict diet, answered and wrote letters, and wanted to live and continue to create art.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pacatte-2017-8)

She died on September 18, 1986, in Watertown Massachusetts at the age of sixty-seven.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Kennelly-2004-21) She left her copyrights and unsold works to the Immaculate Heart Community formed by the former IHM sisters in Los Angeles.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography2-22)

## Artistic style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Artistic style")]

Corita Kent worked at the intersection of several powerful—and at times contradictory—cultural, political, and religious influences. Corita Kent, inspired by the works of [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"), began using [popular culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_culture "Popular culture") as raw material for her work in 1962.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5) Her screen prints often incorporated archetypical product brands of American [consumerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumerism "Consumerism") alongside spiritual texts. Her design process involved appropriating an original advertising graphic to suit her idea; for example, she would tear, rip, or crumple the image, then re-photograph it. She often used grocery store signage, texts from scripture, newspaper clippings, song lyrics, and writings from literary greats such as [Gertrude Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrude_Stein "Gertrude Stein"), [E. E. Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._E._Cummings "E. E. Cummings"), and [Albert Camus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Camus "Albert Camus") as the textual focal point of her work.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-23)

E. E. Cummings was one of Kent's earliest and strongest influences. She quotes him in her work separately more than a dozen times and was inspired by a line from one of his lectures to create an entire series of alphabet prints.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-The_Getty_Iris-2015-13) In her 1966 piece _Tame It's Not_, she uses quotes from Winnie the Pooh, Kierkegaard, and an ad slogan for men's cologne. Using everyday consumer items, like Wonderbread, she was able to bring words and thoughts about her religion to a familiar product that people saw and used every day.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Art_Story-2) By creating juxtaposition between formally acknowledged or respected "art" and the art Corita saw in her everyday world—at the supermarket, on a walk, in the classroom—she elevated the banal to the holy. "Like a priest, a shaman, a magician, she could pass her hands over the commonest of the everyday, the superficial, the oh-so-ordinary, and make it a vehicle of the luminous, the only, and the hope filled," noted Corita's friend, theologian [Harvey Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Cox "Harvey Cox").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-24)

Corita's earliest work was mostly iconographic, drawing inspiration and material from the Bible and other religious sources. Her style is heavily text-based, with scripture passages or positive quotes often encompassing entire compositions with bold and highly saturated typefaces. Despite the often surreal or disorienting compositions of her works, her pieces are "always _about_ something."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dammann-2015-5) By the 1960s, her work started becoming increasingly political.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Corita_Art_Center_Biography-1)

Kent produced her oeuvre during her time at Immaculate Heart College in Los Angeles in response to the Catholic reform in the 1960s by the Vatican Council II as well as several political and social issues happening at the time.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Newhouse-2000-25) Her work itself aided in the Vatican II movement, a movement to modernize and make relevant the Catholic Church. Kent's use of English church texts in her work, for example, made an impact on the Vatican II's efforts to normalize conducting Mass in English.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-26) Because of her strongly political art, she and others left their order to create the Immaculate Heart Community in 1970 to avoid problems with their archdiocese.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Newhouse-2000-25)

The "_Big G_" logo that Kent appropriated from General Mills was to stress the idea of 'goodness', while the elements from Esso gasoline ads were meant to project the internal power within humans.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pagel-2000-27) Unsurprisingly, a Christian subtext does underscore several of her artworks, but not all, which are open to interpretation.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pagel-2000-27)

One of Kent's prints, _love your brother_ (1969), depicts photographs of Martin Luther King Jr. overlaid with her handwritten words, "The king is dead. Love your brother," producing one of her more serious artworks, and presenting her views on politics and human nature.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-28) Her collages took popular images, often with twisted or reversed words, to comment on the political unrest of the period, many of which could have been found at any number of marches or demonstrations, some of which she attended herself.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Pagel-2000-27)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corita_Kent&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

Kent had solo exhibitions at the [National Museum of Women in the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Women_in_the_Arts "National Museum of Women in the Arts") (_R(ad)ical Love: Sister Mary Corita_,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-National_Museum_of_Women_in_the_Arts-29) 2012) and her work is in several art museums, including the [Whitney Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Museum_of_American_Art "Whitney Museum of American Art"), the [Museum of Fine Arts, Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Fine_Arts,_Boston "Museum of Fine Arts, Boston") and [The Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"). An archive is dedicated to her at the [Immaculate Heart Community Headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Heart_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Immaculate Heart High School (Los Angeles)") in Hollywood, CA. Some of Sister Corita's papers and early artwork are in Schlesinger Library, in the Radcliffe Institute, Harvard University.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-30) Recent solo exhibitions of Kent's work include _Someday is Now: The Art of Corita Kent_[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-31) at the Tang Museum at [Skidmore College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore_College "Skidmore College") and _There Will Be New Rules Next Week_ at [Dundee Contemporary Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee_Contemporary_Arts "Dundee Contemporary Arts").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-32)

The Corita Art Center (CAC), a gallery and archive dedicated to preserving and promoting the work and spirit of Corita Kent, was originally founded as the Corita Prints in 1969 in North Hollywood. It changed its name when it moved to the Immaculate Heart property in 1997 and is located within the offices of the Immaculate Heart Community Headquarters in Hollywood, CA.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-33) In September, 2024, the CAC announced that it would move to a new location in the [Arts District of Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_District,_Los_Angeles "Arts District, Los Angeles") in 2025.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-34) The Corita Art Center opened in the Los Angeles Arts District on March 8, 2025.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-35)

Corita Kent received the American Institute of Graphic Arts Medal in 2016.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-Dackerman-36)

Kent was one of the nuns featured in _[Rebel Hearts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel\_Hearts\_(film) "Rebel Hearts (film)")_, a 2021 American documentary directed, produced, and edited by [Pedro Kos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Kos "Pedro Kos"). It had its world premiere at the [2021 Sundance Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Sundance_Film_Festival "2021 Sundance Film Festival") on January 29, 2021.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-37) It received a [limited release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_release "Limited release") on June 25, 2021, before digital streaming on [Discovery+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery+ "Discovery+") starting June 27, 2021.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-38)

In 2023 the Catticus Corporation was granted $700,000[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-39) by the [National Endowment for the Humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Humanities "National Endowment for the Humanities") to produce a documentary, titled "You Should Never Blink", about the rebellious life of the “pop art nun” Corita Kent.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corita_Kent#cite_note-40)

Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_Medalists#cite_note-2) the [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication")."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_Medalists#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.

Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

| Awarded for | Exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication") |
| Presented by | [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) |

| Website | [www.aiga.org](http://www.aiga.org/) |

Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_Medalists#cite_note-2) the [American Institute of Graphic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts") (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design") and [visual communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_communication "Visual communication")."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_Medalists#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.

Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

**David Carson** (born September 8, 1955)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) is an American [graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_designer "Graphic designer") and design director.

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Carson_(graphic_designer)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Carson was born on September 8, 1955, in [Corpus Christi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi,_Texas "Corpus Christi, Texas"), Texas.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) Graduating from [Rolling Hills High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Hills_High_School "Rolling Hills High School"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:1-2) he continued his education and graduated from [San Diego State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_State_University "San Diego State University") with a Bachelor of Arts in [Sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:1-2) Carson attended the Oregon College of Commercial Art studying graphic design and went to Switzerland for a workshop as a part of his degree.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Carson_(graphic_designer)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Carson was a professional [surfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surfing "Surfing") before finding employment with _Self and Musician_ magazine.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) He then worked at _[Transworld Skateboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transworld\_Skateboarding "Transworld Skateboarding")_ for four years. During that time, he became the art director of the magazine and edited their layouts. His 'dirty' photographic techniques emerged during his time there.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3) Carson was then hired as an art director at _Beach Culture_ in 1989.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) Though the magazine ended after six issues, Carson established a reputation for himself.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3)

Three years later Carson was hired by [_Ray Gun_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Gun_(magazine) "Ray Gun (magazine)") magazine, where he stayed for three years. His style was chaotic and [collage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collage "Collage")-like, with layering of photos and messy [typography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typography "Typography"). Most of his work was shown in his covers that were eye-catching with the purpose to visually communicate with everyone, especially young readers and big corporations.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3) During the early 1990s, digital media started to get impacted with Modernism. Carson took advantage of this and stated, "It's the basic decisions—images, cropping and appropriate font and design choices—that make design work, not having the ability to overlap or play with opacity." _Ray Gun_ was the platform that Carson's visual concepts made famous. Looking back to that time Carson explains, "Graphic design seems a bit stagnant now, and a lot of people and ideas have gone to other areas of expression."

Carson later created his own design firm, David Carson Design.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) While working independently, he signed contracts with Nike, Pepsi Cola, Ray Ban, Levi Strauss, and MTC Global. He published a collection of his own graphic works in his books: _The End of Print: The Graphic Design of David Carson_, _2nd Sight, Trek and Fotografiks._[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3)

In 1999, he helped create the cover art and graphics for [Nine Inch Nails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Inch_Nails "Nine Inch Nails")’ [The Fragile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fragile "The Fragile") album.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-4)

## Notable awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Carson_(graphic_designer)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Notable awards")]

Carson received the [AIGA medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_medal "AIGA medal") in 2014.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-5) He received this award for forging graphic design into a cultural form with his own shape and direction.**[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:12-6)**

**David Carson** (born September 8, 1955)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) is an American [graphic designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_designer "Graphic designer") and design director.

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Carson_(graphic_designer)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Carson was born on September 8, 1955, in [Corpus Christi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi,_Texas "Corpus Christi, Texas"), Texas.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) Graduating from [Rolling Hills High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Hills_High_School "Rolling Hills High School"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:1-2) he continued his education and graduated from [San Diego State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_State_University "San Diego State University") with a Bachelor of Arts in [Sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:1-2) Carson attended the Oregon College of Commercial Art studying graphic design and went to Switzerland for a workshop as a part of his degree.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Carson_(graphic_designer)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Carson was a professional [surfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surfing "Surfing") before finding employment with _Self and Musician_ magazine.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) He then worked at _[Transworld Skateboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transworld\_Skateboarding "Transworld Skateboarding")_ for four years. During that time, he became the art director of the magazine and edited their layouts. His 'dirty' photographic techniques emerged during his time there.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3) Carson was then hired as an art director at _Beach Culture_ in 1989.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) Though the magazine ended after six issues, Carson established a reputation for himself.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3)

Three years later Carson was hired by [_Ray Gun_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Gun_(magazine) "Ray Gun (magazine)") magazine, where he stayed for three years. His style was chaotic and [collage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collage "Collage")-like, with layering of photos and messy [typography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typography "Typography"). Most of his work was shown in his covers that were eye-catching with the purpose to visually communicate with everyone, especially young readers and big corporations.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3) During the early 1990s, digital media started to get impacted with Modernism. Carson took advantage of this and stated, "It's the basic decisions—images, cropping and appropriate font and design choices—that make design work, not having the ability to overlap or play with opacity." _Ray Gun_ was the platform that Carson's visual concepts made famous. Looking back to that time Carson explains, "Graphic design seems a bit stagnant now, and a lot of people and ideas have gone to other areas of expression."

Carson later created his own design firm, David Carson Design.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:0-1) While working independently, he signed contracts with Nike, Pepsi Cola, Ray Ban, Levi Strauss, and MTC Global. He published a collection of his own graphic works in his books: _The End of Print: The Graphic Design of David Carson_, _2nd Sight, Trek and Fotografiks._[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:02-3)

In 1999, he helped create the cover art and graphics for [Nine Inch Nails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Inch_Nails "Nine Inch Nails")’ [The Fragile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fragile "The Fragile") album.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-4)

## Notable awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Carson_(graphic_designer)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Notable awards")]

Carson received the [AIGA medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA_medal "AIGA medal") in 2014.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-5) He received this award for forging graphic design into a cultural form with his own shape and direction.**[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)#cite_note-:12-6)**

**Victor Moscoso** (born July 28, 1936)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-1) is a Spanish–American artist best known for producing [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") posters, advertisements, and [underground comix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_comix "Underground comix") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") during the 1960s and 1970s. He was the first of the rock poster artists of the 1960s era with formal academic training and experience. He was the first of the rock poster artists to use photographic collage in many of his posters.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victor_Moscoso&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Moscoso was born in the Vilaboa [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parroquia_(Spain) "Parroquia (Spain)") of [Culleredo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culleredo "Culleredo"), Galicia. He moved with his mother to [Oleiros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleiros,_Galicia "Oleiros, Galicia"). His father, whose parents had already emigrated to [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"), was exiled to the U.S. after being persecuted by the _[falange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FET\_y\_de\_las\_JONS "FET y de las JONS")_. At the age of four, Moscoso and his mother, joined his father, and travelled to [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), where he stayed until he was an adult. His father worked as a [painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_painter_and_decorator "House painter and decorator") and taught him about [color combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_scheme "Color scheme"). His mother was a [seamstress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamstress "Seamstress")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-5)

After studying art at [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union") in New York City and at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), Moscoso moved to [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") in 1959. There, he attended the [San Francisco Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Art_Institute "San Francisco Art Institute"), where he eventually became an instructor.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victor_Moscoso&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Moscoso's use of vibrating colors was influenced by painter [Josef Albers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Albers "Josef Albers"), one of his teachers at Yale.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-7)

Professional success came in the form of the psychedelic rock and roll poster art created for San Francisco and Denver’s dance halls and clubs. Moscoso's posters for the [Family Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Dog_Productions "Family Dog Productions") dance-concerts at the [Avalon Ballroom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalon_Ballroom "Avalon Ballroom") and his Neon Rose posters for the Matrix resulted in international attention during the 1967 [Summer of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_of_Love "Summer of Love").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-auto1-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-10) From September to December 1967, his psychedelic posters done for Chet Helms’ [Family Dog Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Family_Dog_Denver "The Family Dog Denver") further extended his accomplishments and recognition. Moscoso's poster work includes album covers for musicians such as [Jerry Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Garcia "Jerry Garcia"), [Bob Weir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weir "Bob Weir"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Jed Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jed_Davis_(musician) "Jed Davis (musician)"), and [David Grisman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Grisman "David Grisman").

By 1968, Moscoso was doing work for [underground comix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_comix "Underground comix"), for such titles as _[Yellow Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow\_Dog\_(comics) "Yellow Dog (comics)")_, _Jiz Comics_, _Snatch Comics_, _El Perfecto Comics_, and _[Zap Comix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zap\_Comix "Zap Comix")_. As one of the _Zap_ artists, his psychedelic work once again received international attention. His comics appeared in every issue of _Zap_ from 1968 until the title's final issue in 2014; he also illustrated the covers for _Zap_ #s 4, 10, and 13. Moscoso's comix work is notable for its repetitive framing and reliance on an eight-panel grid. The subjects of his comics in _Zap_ are often classic characters like [Mickey Mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mickey_Mouse "Mickey Mouse"), [Donald Duck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Duck "Donald Duck"), [Krazy Kat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krazy_Kat "Krazy Kat"), [Mr. Peanut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Peanut "Mr. Peanut"), [Bugs Bunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugs_Bunny "Bugs Bunny") and [Winsor McCay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winsor_McCay "Winsor McCay")'s [Little Nemo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Nemo "Little Nemo").

In 1977, Moscoso designed radio station [KMEL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KMEL "KMEL")'s mascot: a camel wearing headphones.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-McDonough1980-11) (The station used the KMEL call letters to name itself "Kamel 106".)

Moscoso has also created art for use on [T-shirts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-shirt "T-shirt"), billboards and animated commercials for radio stations, for which he received two [Clio awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clio_award "Clio award").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-12) In addition, he was given an [Inkpot Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkpot_Award "Inkpot Award") in 1979.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-13) Moscoso was a 2018 AIGA Medalist.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-14)

In 1979, the French publisher Futuropolis published _Moscoso Comix_ #1, a 52-page collection (which was republished in English 1989). _Sex, Rock 'N' Roll, & Optical Illusions_, a comprehensive collection of Moscoso's poster and comics work, was published by [Fantagraphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantagraphics "Fantagraphics") in 2006, featuring introductions by [Steven Heller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Heller_(design_writer) "Steven Heller (design writer)") and [Milton Glaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Glaser "Milton Glaser").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-15)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victor_Moscoso&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Moscoso returned to Galicia for the first time in 1965, at age 29. In 2016, he described the visit as "Travelling a 100 years back in time. I could visit my grandparents who were, at the time, very old." Even though he returned sporadically after that, he showed little interest in visiting again, as the last time he did so was in 2001.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-16) As of 2021, Moscoso still lives in the San Francisco Bay Area.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-17)

**Victor Moscoso** (born July 28, 1936)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-1) is a Spanish–American artist best known for producing [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") posters, advertisements, and [underground comix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_comix "Underground comix") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") during the 1960s and 1970s. He was the first of the rock poster artists of the 1960s era with formal academic training and experience. He was the first of the rock poster artists to use photographic collage in many of his posters.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victor_Moscoso&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Moscoso was born in the Vilaboa [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parroquia_(Spain) "Parroquia (Spain)") of [Culleredo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culleredo "Culleredo"), Galicia. He moved with his mother to [Oleiros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleiros,_Galicia "Oleiros, Galicia"). His father, whose parents had already emigrated to [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"), was exiled to the U.S. after being persecuted by the _[falange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FET\_y\_de\_las\_JONS "FET y de las JONS")_. At the age of four, Moscoso and his mother, joined his father, and travelled to [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), where he stayed until he was an adult. His father worked as a [painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_painter_and_decorator "House painter and decorator") and taught him about [color combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_scheme "Color scheme"). His mother was a [seamstress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamstress "Seamstress")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-5)

After studying art at [Cooper Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Union "Cooper Union") in New York City and at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), Moscoso moved to [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") in 1959. There, he attended the [San Francisco Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Art_Institute "San Francisco Art Institute"), where he eventually became an instructor.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victor_Moscoso&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Moscoso's use of vibrating colors was influenced by painter [Josef Albers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Albers "Josef Albers"), one of his teachers at Yale.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-7)

Professional success came in the form of the psychedelic rock and roll poster art created for San Francisco and Denver’s dance halls and clubs. Moscoso's posters for the [Family Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Dog_Productions "Family Dog Productions") dance-concerts at the [Avalon Ballroom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalon_Ballroom "Avalon Ballroom") and his Neon Rose posters for the Matrix resulted in international attention during the 1967 [Summer of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_of_Love "Summer of Love").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-auto1-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-10) From September to December 1967, his psychedelic posters done for Chet Helms’ [Family Dog Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Family_Dog_Denver "The Family Dog Denver") further extended his accomplishments and recognition. Moscoso's poster work includes album covers for musicians such as [Jerry Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Garcia "Jerry Garcia"), [Bob Weir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weir "Bob Weir"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Jed Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jed_Davis_(musician) "Jed Davis (musician)"), and [David Grisman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Grisman "David Grisman").

By 1968, Moscoso was doing work for [underground comix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_comix "Underground comix"), for such titles as _[Yellow Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow\_Dog\_(comics) "Yellow Dog (comics)")_, _Jiz Comics_, _Snatch Comics_, _El Perfecto Comics_, and _[Zap Comix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zap\_Comix "Zap Comix")_. As one of the _Zap_ artists, his psychedelic work once again received international attention. His comics appeared in every issue of _Zap_ from 1968 until the title's final issue in 2014; he also illustrated the covers for _Zap_ #s 4, 10, and 13. Moscoso's comix work is notable for its repetitive framing and reliance on an eight-panel grid. The subjects of his comics in _Zap_ are often classic characters like [Mickey Mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mickey_Mouse "Mickey Mouse"), [Donald Duck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Duck "Donald Duck"), [Krazy Kat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krazy_Kat "Krazy Kat"), [Mr. Peanut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Peanut "Mr. Peanut"), [Bugs Bunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugs_Bunny "Bugs Bunny") and [Winsor McCay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winsor_McCay "Winsor McCay")'s [Little Nemo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Nemo "Little Nemo").

In 1977, Moscoso designed radio station [KMEL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KMEL "KMEL")'s mascot: a camel wearing headphones.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-McDonough1980-11) (The station used the KMEL call letters to name itself "Kamel 106".)

Moscoso has also created art for use on [T-shirts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-shirt "T-shirt"), billboards and animated commercials for radio stations, for which he received two [Clio awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clio_award "Clio award").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-12) In addition, he was given an [Inkpot Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkpot_Award "Inkpot Award") in 1979.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-13) Moscoso was a 2018 AIGA Medalist.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-14)

In 1979, the French publisher Futuropolis published _Moscoso Comix_ #1, a 52-page collection (which was republished in English 1989). _Sex, Rock 'N' Roll, & Optical Illusions_, a comprehensive collection of Moscoso's poster and comics work, was published by [Fantagraphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantagraphics "Fantagraphics") in 2006, featuring introductions by [Steven Heller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Heller_(design_writer) "Steven Heller (design writer)") and [Milton Glaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Glaser "Milton Glaser").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-15)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victor_Moscoso&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Moscoso returned to Galicia for the first time in 1965, at age 29. In 2016, he described the visit as "Travelling a 100 years back in time. I could visit my grandparents who were, at the time, very old." Even though he returned sporadically after that, he showed little interest in visiting again, as the last time he did so was in 2001.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-16) As of 2021, Moscoso still lives in the San Francisco Bay Area.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso#cite_note-17)

# 2014 AIGA Medalist: Sylvia Harris

[AIGA Design Conference](https://www.aiga.org/design/aiga-design-conference)[Learn About the AIGA Medal](https://www.aiga.org/competitions-initiatives/aiga-awards/aiga-medal)

![Image 5: Sylvia Harris](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/full_content_width_320/public/2021-10/Sylvia_Harris.jpg?itok=sY_pS_mV)

**Recognition**  
 2014 AIGA Medal  
**Born**  
 1953, Richmond, Virginia  
**Deceased**  
 2011, Washington, DC

By David Gibson  
 September 8, 2014

Follow Us

[Facebook](https://www.aiga.org/#facebook)[LinkedIn](https://www.aiga.org/#linkedin)[Pinterest](https://www.aiga.org/#pinterest)[X](https://www.aiga.org/#x)[Threads](https://www.aiga.org/#threads)

_Recognized for an unerring commitment to using design to improve the civic experience and for influencing a generation of designers as a teacher and mentor._

Sylvia Harris was a remarkable advocate of good design for real people—a Citizen Designer. She always lived her passions, so it is fitting that she named what was to be the last iteration of her professional practice Citizen Research & Design, which she envisioned as a research and planning firm designed to help public sector organizations better communicate with the people they serve.

The 2011 rebranding and repositioning of her firm, formerly Sylvia Harris LLC, was intended to help her achieve two things. On the one hand, Harris wanted to dig deeper into the field of research—to conduct rigorous investigations that would help organizations understand how people actually experience design systems. With that research in hand, she could set in motion intelligent plans for large-scale public design programs. At the same time, she wanted to build a practice that was bigger than herself—a band of citizens who would use their expertise on behalf of the common good. Although Harris had already accomplished a great deal in her life, her ambitious idea and new direction were cut short by her sudden and untimely death on July 24, 2011.

![Image 6: ACLU brand identity](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_03_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### ACLU brand identity, 2002 Client: American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU); Design firm: The Wilson Group; Creative director: Fo Wilson; Art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Leila Taylor.

![Image 7: Sylvia Harris (Photo: George Larkins)](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/harris_sylvia_portrait_by_george_larkins_640.jpg)

###### Sylvia Harris (Photo: George Larkins).

![Image 8: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts Environmental Branding Study, 2000 Client: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; Design firms: Sylvia Harris LLC, Cooper Robertson & Partners, Pentagram Design; Creative director: Michael Bierut; Art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Rion Byrd](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_02_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts Environmental Branding Study, 2000 Client: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; Design firms: Sylvia Harris LLC, Cooper Robertson & Partners, Pentagram Design; Creative director: Michael Bierut; Art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Rion Byrd.

Harris’ journey began in her hometown of Richmond, Virginia. As a young black woman in the South during the 1960s, she experienced desegregation firsthand and, in the process, gained a visceral understanding of how social systems affect people’s daily lives. She cultivated an interest in design while studying with AIGA Medalist Philip B. Meggs at Virginia Commonwealth University, where she received a B.F.A. in 1975. A move to Boston to work with architects and in broadcast media was formative in opening her eyes to the depth and diversity of graphic design practice. At the WGBH design department, Chris Pullman, another AIGA Medalist, became a mentor and catalyst for her enrollment in the master’s program in graphic design at Yale University.

Right after graduating from Yale, in 1980, Harris cofounded Two Twelve Associates with classmates Juanita Dugdale and myself. While dealing with the challenges of building a new design practice, she honed the skills and interests that would ultimately propel her career. As the projects became larger and more complex, she relentlessly explored how to use all of the tools in a designer’s tool kit to create comprehensive public information systems. Her groundbreaking work in digital consumer banking systems for Citibank set an early standard for human-centered automated customer service.

![Image 9: Columbia University Environmental Branding](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_fourth_width_320/public/l_04_harris_portimage_640.jpg?itok=NukK5WJI)

###### Columbia University Environmental Branding and Wayfinding Study, 2004 Client: Columbia University, Office of Facilities Management; Design firm: Sylvia Harris LLC; Creative director and art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Sally Minker.

![Image 10: Aetna calendar](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_05_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### Aetna calendar, 1996 Client: Aetna Insurance Company; Design firm: Two Twelve Associates, Inc.; Creative director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Julie Marable; Photographers: Bert Andrews, Susan Wides.

![Image 11: Voting By Design poster](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_fourth_width_320/public/l_08_harris_shllc_images_640.jpg?itok=_s0TOcDi)

###### Voting By Design poster, 2003 Client: University of Minnesota Design Institute; Design firm: Sylvia Harris LLC; Creative directors: Janet Abrams, Sylvia Harris; Designers: Kathleen Meaney, Leila Taylor.

![Image 12: Citibank ATM interaction design](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_07_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### Citibank ATM interaction design, 1989 Client: Citibank Corporation; Design firm: Two Twelve Associates; Creative director and art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: David Peters.

At Sylvia Harris LLC, which she established in 1994 after leaving Two Twelve, she shifted her focus to design planning and strategy. In the process, she guided some of the nation’s largest hospitals, universities and civic agencies through systems planning, policy development and innovation management. As creative director for the United States Census Bureau, Census 2000, she was tasked with encouraging more Americans—including those who had been previously under-represented—to participate. Distributed to 80 million households, the 2000 Census presented an opportunity to study how a redesigned form might boost participation as well as public awareness of the Census brand.

Harris was a woman of great energy, passion and intelligence. She nurtured these qualities by reaching out beyond the walls of her studio. She had a remarkable ability to draw smart, talented young people into her network, making them collaborators and friends. And she generously gave back to the design community that she so vibrantly inhabited for more than three decades, mentoring students as a faculty member of Yale’s graphic design program and as a teacher at the School of Visual Arts, Cooper Union and Purchase College. She also served on the U.S. Postal Service’s Citizens’ Stamp Advisory Committee.

As a designer and a woman, Sylvia Harris always wanted to do the right thing, the smart thing, the thing that would make the biggest difference to the most people. She was the model citizen—a Citizen Designer.

# 2014 AIGA Medalist: Sylvia Harris

[AIGA Design Conference](https://www.aiga.org/design/aiga-design-conference)[Learn About the AIGA Medal](https://www.aiga.org/competitions-initiatives/aiga-awards/aiga-medal)

![Image 5: Sylvia Harris](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/full_content_width_320/public/2021-10/Sylvia_Harris.jpg?itok=sY_pS_mV)

**Recognition**  
 2014 AIGA Medal  
**Born**  
 1953, Richmond, Virginia  
**Deceased**  
 2011, Washington, DC

By David Gibson  
 September 8, 2014

Follow Us

[Facebook](https://www.aiga.org/#facebook)[LinkedIn](https://www.aiga.org/#linkedin)[Pinterest](https://www.aiga.org/#pinterest)[X](https://www.aiga.org/#x)[Threads](https://www.aiga.org/#threads)

_Recognized for an unerring commitment to using design to improve the civic experience and for influencing a generation of designers as a teacher and mentor._

Sylvia Harris was a remarkable advocate of good design for real people—a Citizen Designer. She always lived her passions, so it is fitting that she named what was to be the last iteration of her professional practice Citizen Research & Design, which she envisioned as a research and planning firm designed to help public sector organizations better communicate with the people they serve.

The 2011 rebranding and repositioning of her firm, formerly Sylvia Harris LLC, was intended to help her achieve two things. On the one hand, Harris wanted to dig deeper into the field of research—to conduct rigorous investigations that would help organizations understand how people actually experience design systems. With that research in hand, she could set in motion intelligent plans for large-scale public design programs. At the same time, she wanted to build a practice that was bigger than herself—a band of citizens who would use their expertise on behalf of the common good. Although Harris had already accomplished a great deal in her life, her ambitious idea and new direction were cut short by her sudden and untimely death on July 24, 2011.

![Image 6: ACLU brand identity](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_03_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### ACLU brand identity, 2002 Client: American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU); Design firm: The Wilson Group; Creative director: Fo Wilson; Art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Leila Taylor.

![Image 7: Sylvia Harris (Photo: George Larkins)](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/harris_sylvia_portrait_by_george_larkins_640.jpg)

###### Sylvia Harris (Photo: George Larkins).

![Image 8: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts Environmental Branding Study, 2000 Client: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; Design firms: Sylvia Harris LLC, Cooper Robertson & Partners, Pentagram Design; Creative director: Michael Bierut; Art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Rion Byrd](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_02_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts Environmental Branding Study, 2000 Client: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; Design firms: Sylvia Harris LLC, Cooper Robertson & Partners, Pentagram Design; Creative director: Michael Bierut; Art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Rion Byrd.

Harris’ journey began in her hometown of Richmond, Virginia. As a young black woman in the South during the 1960s, she experienced desegregation firsthand and, in the process, gained a visceral understanding of how social systems affect people’s daily lives. She cultivated an interest in design while studying with AIGA Medalist Philip B. Meggs at Virginia Commonwealth University, where she received a B.F.A. in 1975. A move to Boston to work with architects and in broadcast media was formative in opening her eyes to the depth and diversity of graphic design practice. At the WGBH design department, Chris Pullman, another AIGA Medalist, became a mentor and catalyst for her enrollment in the master’s program in graphic design at Yale University.

Right after graduating from Yale, in 1980, Harris cofounded Two Twelve Associates with classmates Juanita Dugdale and myself. While dealing with the challenges of building a new design practice, she honed the skills and interests that would ultimately propel her career. As the projects became larger and more complex, she relentlessly explored how to use all of the tools in a designer’s tool kit to create comprehensive public information systems. Her groundbreaking work in digital consumer banking systems for Citibank set an early standard for human-centered automated customer service.

![Image 9: Columbia University Environmental Branding](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_fourth_width_320/public/l_04_harris_portimage_640.jpg?itok=NukK5WJI)

###### Columbia University Environmental Branding and Wayfinding Study, 2004 Client: Columbia University, Office of Facilities Management; Design firm: Sylvia Harris LLC; Creative director and art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Sally Minker.

![Image 10: Aetna calendar](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_05_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### Aetna calendar, 1996 Client: Aetna Insurance Company; Design firm: Two Twelve Associates, Inc.; Creative director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: Julie Marable; Photographers: Bert Andrews, Susan Wides.

![Image 11: Voting By Design poster](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_fourth_width_320/public/l_08_harris_shllc_images_640.jpg?itok=_s0TOcDi)

###### Voting By Design poster, 2003 Client: University of Minnesota Design Institute; Design firm: Sylvia Harris LLC; Creative directors: Janet Abrams, Sylvia Harris; Designers: Kathleen Meaney, Leila Taylor.

![Image 12: Citibank ATM interaction design](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/l_07_harris_portimage_640.jpg)

###### Citibank ATM interaction design, 1989 Client: Citibank Corporation; Design firm: Two Twelve Associates; Creative director and art director: Sylvia Harris; Designer: David Peters.

At Sylvia Harris LLC, which she established in 1994 after leaving Two Twelve, she shifted her focus to design planning and strategy. In the process, she guided some of the nation’s largest hospitals, universities and civic agencies through systems planning, policy development and innovation management. As creative director for the United States Census Bureau, Census 2000, she was tasked with encouraging more Americans—including those who had been previously under-represented—to participate. Distributed to 80 million households, the 2000 Census presented an opportunity to study how a redesigned form might boost participation as well as public awareness of the Census brand.

Harris was a woman of great energy, passion and intelligence. She nurtured these qualities by reaching out beyond the walls of her studio. She had a remarkable ability to draw smart, talented young people into her network, making them collaborators and friends. And she generously gave back to the design community that she so vibrantly inhabited for more than three decades, mentoring students as a faculty member of Yale’s graphic design program and as a teacher at the School of Visual Arts, Cooper Union and Purchase College. She also served on the U.S. Postal Service’s Citizens’ Stamp Advisory Committee.

As a designer and a woman, Sylvia Harris always wanted to do the right thing, the smart thing, the thing that would make the biggest difference to the most people. She was the model citizen—a Citizen Designer.

# AIGA Medal

The medal of AIGA—the most distinguished honor in the profession of communication design—has been awarded since 1920 to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements to the advancement of the field of design as a respected craft, strategic advantage, and vital cultural force. Medals have been awarded to individuals who have set standards of excellence over a lifetime of work or have made individual contributions to innovation within the practice of design.

![Image 6: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Maria Giudice](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/maria_giudice_-_1200x1200.png?itok=v09XL_PP)

### Maria Giudice

Maria Giudice is a visionary design leader, entrepreneur, and mentor known for advancing human-centered design in business. As founder and CEO of Hot Studio, she built one of the industry’s first experience design firms, nurturing creative talent that now leads teams across top global companies. After Hot Studio’s acquisition by Facebook, she led large-scale design organizations at Facebook and Autodesk, shaping digital experiences used worldwide. Today, Giudice focuses on developing the next generation of creative leaders through coaching, speaking, and authorship. The co-author of Rise of the DEO and Changemakers, she continues to influence design leadership while pursuing her passion for calligraphy and painting.

![Image 7: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Rick Griffith](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/rick_griffith_-_1200_x_1200_0.png?itok=sXJiEsbB)

### Rick Griffith

Rick Griffith is a British-West Indian–born, Denver-based designer, letterpress printer, and cultural worker known for his bold, typographically driven approach to design and his commitment to social justice. As co-founder of MATTER, a design studio and print shop, he creates work that intersects politics, community, and craft, using design as both a tool and a provocation. Griffith’s posters, installations, and public projects challenge audiences to engage critically with civic life. A frequent lecturer, educator, and curator, he champions design’s power to shape culture and public imagination. His practice is defined by purpose, experimentation, and an unwavering belief in the value of thoughtful communication.

![Image 8: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Elizabeth Resnick](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/elizabeth_resnick_-_1200x1200.png?itok=2m1gHZG1)

### Elizabeth Resnick

Elizabeth Resnick is a Professor Emerita at MassArt and an influential designer, educator, curator, and author. Her independent studio, active from 1973 to 1996, served corporate, nonprofit, and cultural clients across the Boston region. Resnick is internationally recognized for curating major poster exhibitions addressing social justice, peace, AIDS awareness, and gender-based inequality. She has authored or edited numerous books, including Women Graphic Designers: Rebalancing the Canon and The Social Design Reader. A prolific writer and scholar, her work has appeared in EYE, IDEA, Graphis, and more. Resnick has lectured and led workshops worldwide, championing design’s role in culture and social change.

![Image 9: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Dorothy Hayes](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/dorothy_hayes_-_1200x1200.png?itok=e7S6-HsN)

### Dorothy Hayes

Dorothy Hayes (1935–2015) was a pioneering graphic designer, educator, and advocate whose work helped expand the visibility of Black artists in the design field. A graduate of the School of Visual Arts, she built a respected career in corporate design while championing equity and representation in the arts. In 1970, she founded Black Artists in Graphic Communication, a landmark exhibition celebrating the contributions of Black designers nationwide. Hayes later taught at Hostos Community College, inspiring generations with her commitment to creativity, rigor, and opportunity. Her legacy endures through the communities she uplifted and the pathways she opened.

Purpose and Goals

*   To celebrate designers who represent the highest aspirations of our members by honoring inspirational individuals who have successfully enhanced the value and deepened the impact of design on business, society, and culture, through their unique and outstanding contributions in the practice of design, teaching, writing, or leadership of the profession.
*   To increase public awareness and understanding of the critical and influential role of design and designers in business, culture, and our communities at large.

Nominations

AIGA members are invited to submit nominations to be considered by next year’s committee. **To nominate an inspirational colleague, mentor, or individual who **has made a significant impact in the U.S.,** simply complete the[nomination form](https://aiga-awards.secure-platform.com/a/ "AIGA Medalist Nomination Form").** Include the name of the nominee, a short paragraph about why the individual should be considered, and a link to their website or portfolio.Nominations are accepted on a rolling basis and are considered year after year for the next awards cycle. Each year, nominations for the AIGA Medal are reviewed by an awards committee to verify eligibility. Yearly recommendations for Medal awards are then presented to the AIGA National Board of Directors for majority approval. The Board approves a slate of Medalists, and does not propose or reject individual names recommended by the committee.

Individuals who are honored may work in any country, but the contribution for which they are honored should have had a significant impact on the practice of communication design in the United States.

Lens for Unique and Outstanding Contribution

*   **Achievement**: With a focus on craft, eligible nominees will have made a historically significant contribution to the profession
*   **Enrichment**: With a focus on community, eligible nominees will have set a new benchmark for service as community catalysts
*   **Expansion**: With a focus on possibility, nominees will have pushed the envelope to broaden the scope of what we consider great design

Selection Criteria

**The AIGA board of directors has issued the following instructions:**

*   Minimum of one and maximum of three medals will be awarded each year
*   As a whole, the select group of Medalists should represent the design community’s diversity of design practice, gender, ethnicity, and geography
*   While AIGA’s roots are founded in traditional forms of graphic design, the selected group of awardees should reflect the broad scope of where the profession of design is today
*   Honor designers as exemplary, living role models of inspiration and aspiration to our members

One Honorary Medal per year may be awarded at the discretion of the committee to recognize a designer posthumously. Recognition opportunities for posthumous awards may vary.

**Additional attributes for consideration:**

*   Exemplary service to AIGA and the broader design community
*   Strong leader and role model for AIGA’s members and its mission of design as a professional craft, strategic advantage, and vital cultural force
*   Public advocacy for the profession
*   Consistent commitment to social change

# AIGA Medal

The medal of AIGA—the most distinguished honor in the profession of communication design—has been awarded since 1920 to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements to the advancement of the field of design as a respected craft, strategic advantage, and vital cultural force. Medals have been awarded to individuals who have set standards of excellence over a lifetime of work or have made individual contributions to innovation within the practice of design.

## 2025 AIGA Medalists

![Image 6: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Maria Giudice](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/maria_giudice_-_1200x1200.png?itok=v09XL_PP)

### Maria Giudice

Maria Giudice is a visionary design leader, entrepreneur, and mentor known for advancing human-centered design in business. As founder and CEO of Hot Studio, she built one of the industry’s first experience design firms, nurturing creative talent that now leads teams across top global companies. After Hot Studio’s acquisition by Facebook, she led large-scale design organizations at Facebook and Autodesk, shaping digital experiences used worldwide. Today, Giudice focuses on developing the next generation of creative leaders through coaching, speaking, and authorship. The co-author of Rise of the DEO and Changemakers, she continues to influence design leadership while pursuing her passion for calligraphy and painting.

![Image 7: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Rick Griffith](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/rick_griffith_-_1200_x_1200_0.png?itok=sXJiEsbB)

### Rick Griffith

Rick Griffith is a British-West Indian–born, Denver-based designer, letterpress printer, and cultural worker known for his bold, typographically driven approach to design and his commitment to social justice. As co-founder of MATTER, a design studio and print shop, he creates work that intersects politics, community, and craft, using design as both a tool and a provocation. Griffith’s posters, installations, and public projects challenge audiences to engage critically with civic life. A frequent lecturer, educator, and curator, he champions design’s power to shape culture and public imagination. His practice is defined by purpose, experimentation, and an unwavering belief in the value of thoughtful communication.

![Image 8: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Elizabeth Resnick](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/elizabeth_resnick_-_1200x1200.png?itok=2m1gHZG1)

### Elizabeth Resnick

Elizabeth Resnick is a Professor Emerita at MassArt and an influential designer, educator, curator, and author. Her independent studio, active from 1973 to 1996, served corporate, nonprofit, and cultural clients across the Boston region. Resnick is internationally recognized for curating major poster exhibitions addressing social justice, peace, AIDS awareness, and gender-based inequality. She has authored or edited numerous books, including Women Graphic Designers: Rebalancing the Canon and The Social Design Reader. A prolific writer and scholar, her work has appeared in EYE, IDEA, Graphis, and more. Resnick has lectured and led workshops worldwide, championing design’s role in culture and social change.

![Image 9: Headshot of 2025 AIGA Medalist Dorothy Hayes](https://www.aiga.org/sites/default/files/styles/one_third_width_320/public/2025-11/dorothy_hayes_-_1200x1200.png?itok=e7S6-HsN)

### Dorothy Hayes

Dorothy Hayes (1935–2015) was a pioneering graphic designer, educator, and advocate whose work helped expand the visibility of Black artists in the design field. A graduate of the School of Visual Arts, she built a respected career in corporate design while championing equity and representation in the arts. In 1970, she founded Black Artists in Graphic Communication, a landmark exhibition celebrating the contributions of Black designers nationwide. Hayes later taught at Hostos Community College, inspiring generations with her commitment to creativity, rigor, and opportunity. Her legacy endures through the communities she uplifted and the pathways she opened.

Purpose and Goals

*   To celebrate designers who represent the highest aspirations of our members by honoring inspirational individuals who have successfully enhanced the value and deepened the impact of design on business, society, and culture, through their unique and outstanding contributions in the practice of design, teaching, writing, or leadership of the profession.
*   To increase public awareness and understanding of the critical and influential role of design and designers in business, culture, and our communities at large.

Nominations

AIGA members are invited to submit nominations to be considered by next year’s committee. **To nominate an inspirational colleague, mentor, or individual who **has made a significant impact in the U.S.,** simply complete the[nomination form](https://aiga-awards.secure-platform.com/a/ "AIGA Medalist Nomination Form").** Include the name of the nominee, a short paragraph about why the individual should be considered, and a link to their website or portfolio.Nominations are accepted on a rolling basis and are considered year after year for the next awards cycle. Each year, nominations for the AIGA Medal are reviewed by an awards committee to verify eligibility. Yearly recommendations for Medal awards are then presented to the AIGA National Board of Directors for majority approval. The Board approves a slate of Medalists, and does not propose or reject individual names recommended by the committee.

Individuals who are honored may work in any country, but the contribution for which they are honored should have had a significant impact on the practice of communication design in the United States.

Lens for Unique and Outstanding Contribution

*   **Achievement**: With a focus on craft, eligible nominees will have made a historically significant contribution to the profession
*   **Enrichment**: With a focus on community, eligible nominees will have set a new benchmark for service as community catalysts
*   **Expansion**: With a focus on possibility, nominees will have pushed the envelope to broaden the scope of what we consider great design

Selection Criteria

**The AIGA board of directors has issued the following instructions:**

*   Minimum of one and maximum of three medals will be awarded each year
*   As a whole, the select group of Medalists should represent the design community’s diversity of design practice, gender, ethnicity, and geography
*   While AIGA’s roots are founded in traditional forms of graphic design, the selected group of awardees should reflect the broad scope of where the profession of design is today
*   Honor designers as exemplary, living role models of inspiration and aspiration to our members

One Honorary Medal per year may be awarded at the discretion of the committee to recognize a designer posthumously. Recognition opportunities for posthumous awards may vary.

**Additional attributes for consideration:**

*   Exemplary service to AIGA and the broader design community
*   Strong leader and role model for AIGA’s members and its mission of design as a professional craft, strategic advantage, and vital cultural force
*   Public advocacy for the profession
*   Consistent commitment to social change
